stem: After votes in 1997, Scotland and Wales got their own elected bodies, which began work in 1999.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Assembly (now the Senedd) were set up in 1999, with powers over matters such as health and education.

stem: In 1956, British and French forces tried to take control of a canal in which country, leading to a major political crisis?
options: *Egypt | Panama | Turkey | Greece
explanation: The Suez Crisis of 1956 happened when Britain and France invaded Egypt to control the Suez Canal. It showed that Britain was no longer a global superpower.

stem: In 1982, Britain went to war with Argentina over which islands in the South Atlantic?
options: *The Falkland Islands | The Shetland Islands | The Channel Islands | The Cayman Islands
explanation: The Falklands War began after Argentina invaded the islands in April 1982. British forces successfully took back control of the islands.

stem: Which TWO social changes became law in the UK during the 1960s?
options: *Decriminalisation of homosexuality | *Abolition of the death penalty | Votes for women over 21 | Introduction of the state pension
explanation: During the 1960s, Parliament passed laws that decriminalised homosexuality (for men over 21) and ended the death penalty for murder in Great Britain.

stem: In 1971, the UK changed its currency so that there were 100 pence in every pound.
options: *True | False
explanation: On 'Decimal Day' in February 1971, the UK officially changed to decimal currency. Before this, there were 240 pence (or 20 shillings) in a pound.

stem: Which British scientist co-developed the MRI scanner, used in hospitals to take pictures inside the body?
options: *Sir Peter Mansfield | Sir Alexander Fleming | John Logie Baird | Francis Crick
explanation: Sir Peter Mansfield helped develop the MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) scanner, which has saved many lives. He won a Nobel Prize for this work in 2003.

stem: Who was the Prime Minister that led the Labour government elected immediately after the end of World War II in 1945?
options: *Clement Attlee | Winston Churchill | Harold Macmillan | Anthony Eden
explanation: Clement Attlee won a landslide victory in July 1945. His government introduced major social reforms, including the National Health Service.

stem: Nine countries, including India and Pakistan, became independent from British rule between 1947 and 1948.
options: *True | False
explanation: After the Second World War, the British Empire began to break up. India, Pakistan, and seven other nations gained their independence in 1947 and 1948.

stem: In which year was the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II held?
explanation: Queen Elizabeth II came to the throne in 1952 when her father died, but her coronation took place the following year in 1953.

stem: What law passed in 1970 made it illegal to pay women less than men for doing the same job?
options: *The Equal Pay Act | The Gender Equality Bill | The Fair Wage Agreement | The Sex Discrimination Order
explanation: The Equal Pay Act 1970 gave women the legal right to receive the same pay and working conditions as men doing the same or similar work.

stem: Which TWO public services were disrupted by major strikes during the 'Winter of Discontent' in late 1978 and early 1979?
options: *Waste collection | *Gravedigging | Military flights | Television broadcasting
explanation: During the Winter of Discontent, strikes by public sector workers left rubbish uncollected in the streets and meant some graves could not be dug.

stem: Which political leader became Prime Minister in 1997 after branding his party as 'New Labour'?
options: *Tony Blair | Gordon Brown | John Major | Neil Kinnock
explanation: Tony Blair led the Labour Party to a landslide election victory in 1997 under the slogan 'New Labour'.

stem: In 1984, the government of Margaret Thatcher faced a major year-long strike by workers from which industry?
options: *Coal mining | Steel manufacturing | Railway transport | Postal services
explanation: The 1984-1985 miners' strike was a major industrial dispute over the closure of coal mines, which ended in defeat for the miners' union.

stem: Which TWO of these places were built as part of the 'new towns' program started by the government in 1946?
options: *Milton Keynes | *Stevenage | Manchester | Birmingham
explanation: The New Towns Act 1946 led to the creation of completely new, planned communities like Stevenage, Milton Keynes, and Cwmbran to rebuild post-war Britain.

stem: In 1960, which Prime Minister gave a famous speech about the 'wind of change' blowing through Africa, referring to decolonisation?
options: *Harold Macmillan | Winston Churchill | Edward Heath | James Callaghan
explanation: Harold Macmillan's 'wind of change' speech in South Africa in 1960 recognised that African nations wanted and would get independence from the Empire.

stem: Who succeeded Margaret Thatcher as Prime Minister in 1990?
options: *John Major | Tony Blair | Harold Wilson | James Callaghan
explanation: John Major served as Prime Minister from 1990 to 1997. He was leader of the Conservative Party during this time.

stem: In which year did scientists Francis Crick and James Watson discover the structure of the DNA molecule?
explanation: The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953. This work took place at the University of Cambridge.

stem: The UK was one of the original members of NATO, which was signed in 1949.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK was a founder member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) in 1949. This is an alliance of nations committed to mutual defence.

stem: What famous radio telescope, built in Cheshire in 1957, was the biggest in the world at that time?
options: *Jodrell Bank | Greenwich Observatory | Royal Observatory | Eden Project
explanation: Sir Bernard Lovell built the Jodrell Bank radio telescope in Cheshire. For many years, it was the largest radio telescope in the world.

stem: Which TWO countries did British forces fight in during the 2000s as part of international campaigns against terrorism?
options: *Iraq | *Afghanistan | Vietnam | Argentina
explanation: British forces operated alongside global allies in Afghanistan from 2001 and Iraq from 2003 to help fight international terrorism.

stem: Which Prime Minister's government established the Open University in 1969 to offer higher education to more people?
options: *Harold Wilson | Edward Heath | James Callaghan | Clement Attlee
explanation: Harold Wilson's Labour government introduced the Open University in 1969. It allowed people to study for degrees through distance learning.

stem: In 1975, the UK held a national referendum and voted to stay in the European Common Market.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK joined the European Economic Community (Common Market) in 1973. In 1975, a referendum was held, and the public voted to remain a member.

stem: Following the general election in 2010, which two political parties formed a coalition government?
options: *Conservatives and Liberal Democrats | Labour and Liberal Democrats | Conservatives and UKIP | Labour and the Scottish National Party
explanation: No single political party won a majority in the 2010 election. The Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats agreed to form a coalition government.

stem: What famous ship arrived in Britain in 1948, bringing people from the West Indies to help rebuild the country?
options: *Empire Windrush | Queen Mary | Titanic | Cutty Sark
explanation: The Empire Windrush brought passengers from Jamaica in 1948. Many people from the Commonwealth came to live and work in the UK after World War II.

stem: Who became Prime Minister in 2007 after Tony Blair resigned?
options: *Gordon Brown | David Cameron | Theresa May | John Major
explanation: Gordon Brown served as Prime Minister from 2007 until the general election in 2010. He belonged to the Labour Party.

stem: In 2012, which major international sporting event did London host for the third time?
options: *The Olympic Games | The FIFA World Cup | The Commonwealth Games | The Rugby World Cup
explanation: London hosted the Olympic Games in 2012. It was the third time the city had hosted the games, having previously done so in 1908 and 1948.

stem: Which TWO of these Jubilees did Queen Elizabeth II celebrate to mark 25 years and 50 years on the throne?
options: *Silver Jubilee | *Golden Jubilee | Diamond Jubilee | Platinum Jubilee
explanation: Queen Elizabeth II celebrated her Silver Jubilee (25 years) in 1977 and her Golden Jubilee (50 years) in 2002. She later celebrated her Diamond Jubilee in 2012.

stem: What famous report in 1942 recommended the creation of a welfare state to fight poverty and unemployment in Britain?
options: *The Beveridge Report | The Butler Report | The Macmillan Report | The Attlee Report
explanation: William Beveridge wrote the report in 1942, recommending that the government fight five 'giant evils'. This led to major post-war reforms.

stem: In 1969, why were British troops sent to Northern Ireland?
options: *To keep peace between Protestant and Catholic communities | To defend the border against an invasion from Ireland | To rebuild roads and schools after a natural disaster | To train the local police force in modern fighting methods
explanation: British troops were sent to Northern Ireland in 1969 to maintain order after serious sectarian rioting broke out between the two communities.

stem: Which conflict in 1991 did British forces play a major role in, helping to liberate Kuwait?
options: *The Gulf War | The Korean War | The Suez Crisis | The Falklands War
explanation: In 1991, British troops joined an international coalition in the Gulf War. They successfully liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.

stem: In which year was the Festival of Britain held to celebrate the country's recovery after World War II?
explanation: The Festival of Britain was held in 1951, exactly 100 years after the Great Exhibition of 1851. It aimed to show Britain's progress in science, technology, and the arts after the war.

stem: During the 1980s, the government led by Margaret Thatcher worked to privatise state-owned businesses. What does "privatise" mean?
options: *Sell them to private buyers | Close them down permanently | Merge them into one big department | Move them to other countries
explanation: The Conservative government under Margaret Thatcher privatised many state-run national industries, such as gas, electricity, and telecommunications, by selling them to private buyers.

stem: Queen Elizabeth II became queen in 1952 following the death of her father, King George VI.
options: *True | False
explanation: Although her coronation took place in 1953, Elizabeth II officially became Queen in 1952 when her father, King George VI, passed away.

stem: Who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1976 for their work to end the violence in Northern Ireland?
options: John Hume and David Trimble | *Mairead Corrigan and Betty Williams | Tony Blair and Bertie Ahern | Harold Wilson and Edward Heath
explanation: Mairead Corrigan and Betty Williams founded the Northern Ireland Peace Movement (Peace People) and were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1976 for their peace efforts.

stem: Which TWO popular British rock bands became world-famous during the cultural movement known as the "Swinging Sixties"?
options: *The Beatles | *The Rolling Stones | Coldplay | Oasis
explanation: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were key parts of the cultural boom of the 1960s, known as the "Swinging Sixties", which made British music popular worldwide.

stem: In 2012, Queen Elizabeth II celebrated her Diamond Jubilee. How many years on the throne did this mark?
options: 50 years | *60 years | 70 years | 75 years
explanation: A Diamond Jubilee marks 60 years of a monarch's reign. Queen Elizabeth II celebrated this milestone in 2012, the same year London hosted the Olympic Games.

stem: In 2013, the UK Parliament passed a law that allowed same-sex couples to do what in England and Wales?
options: *Marry each other | Adopt children | Jointly open a bank account | Vote in general elections
explanation: The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act was passed by Parliament in 2013, making same-sex marriage legal in England and Wales. Equal marriage laws were passed in Scotland in 2014.

stem: The UK is one of five permanent members of the United Nations (UN) Security Council. Which TWO other countries are also permanent members?
options: *United States | *France | Germany | Japan
explanation: The UN Security Council has five permanent members with veto power: the UK, the United States, France, China, and Russia. It was established after World War II.

stem: Which British Prime Minister led the UK into the European Economic Community (EEC) in 1973?
options: Harold Wilson | *Edward Heath | James Callaghan | Margaret Thatcher
explanation: Edward Heath was the Conservative Prime Minister who successfully negotiated the UK's entry into the European Economic Community (EEC) in 1973.

stem: As the British Empire dismantled after World War II, most of the newly independent countries joined which international organisation?
options: *The Commonwealth | The European Union | The League of Nations | The United Nations Security Council
explanation: As Britain granted independence to its colonies, a voluntary association of independent countries called the Commonwealth was formed, with the British monarch as its head.

stem: Which king broke away from the Church of Rome?
options: *Henry VIII | Edward I | Charles II | James I
explanation: Henry VIII set up the Church of England when the Pope would not let him end his first marriage.

stem: Which of Henry VIII's wives gave birth to his only son, Edward?
options: *Jane Seymour | Anne Boleyn | Catherine of Aragon | Catherine Parr
explanation: Jane Seymour gave Henry VIII the son he wanted, who became Edward VI. She died soon after the birth.

stem: In 1588, which fleet did the English defeat?
options: *The Spanish Armada | The French navy | The Dutch fleet | The Viking fleet
explanation: The English defeated the Spanish Armada, a large fleet of ships sent to invade England and bring back the Catholic faith.

stem: Who was the monarch when the Spanish Armada was defeated?
options: *Elizabeth I | Mary I | Victoria | Anne
explanation: Elizabeth I was queen when the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588. She was very popular and her reign is often remembered as a golden age.

stem: Where was William Shakespeare born?
options: *Stratford-upon-Avon | London | Oxford | Canterbury
explanation: William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564. Many people think he is the greatest writer in the English language.

stem: Which king of Scotland also became King of England in 1603?
options: *James VI | Charles I | Robert the Bruce | William III
explanation: When Elizabeth I died without children, James VI of Scotland became James I of England. He ruled both countries.

stem: Which king was executed in 1649 after the English Civil War?
options: *Charles I | Charles II | James II | Henry VIII
explanation: Charles I lost the Civil War against Parliament and was executed in 1649. England became a republic for a short time.

stem: In the English Civil War, what were supporters of the king called?
options: *Cavaliers | Roundheads | Jacobites | Puritans
explanation: Supporters of the king were called Cavaliers. Supporters of Parliament were called Roundheads.

stem: Who became Lord Protector after the English Civil War?
options: *Oliver Cromwell | Robert Walpole | Thomas Cromwell | William of Orange
explanation: Oliver Cromwell led the army of Parliament and ruled England as Lord Protector until he died in 1658.

stem: In which year was there a great fire in London?
explanation: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed many buildings. Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.

stem: What was the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
options: *William of Orange became king with no fighting in England | Parliament got rid of the monarchy | Scotland and England joined together | Charles II came back from exile
explanation: Protestant leaders invited William of Orange to take the throne. James II fled to France and there was no fighting in England, so it was called glorious.

stem: The Act of Union of 1707 joined England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Act of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain. Scotland kept its own legal and education systems and its own church.

stem: Which law of 1679 protects people from being held in prison unlawfully?
options: *The Habeas Corpus Act | The Bill of Rights | The Magna Carta | The Act of Union
explanation: The Habeas Corpus Act means someone who is arrested must be brought before a court. This protects people from being held without a lawful reason.

stem: Which queen tried to make England a Catholic country again after King Edward VI died?
options: *Mary I | Elizabeth I | Queen Anne | Queen Victoria
explanation: Queen Mary I was very religious and wanted the country to be Catholic. She killed many Protestants, so people called her 'Bloody Mary'.

stem: In 1620, a group of people called the Pilgrims left for North America on which ship?
options: *The Mayflower | The Golden Hind | The Mary Rose | The Victory
explanation: The Pilgrims were looking for religious freedom. They sailed on the Mayflower and started a colony in what is now the United States.

stem: Who was a famous scientist during the Stuart period who discovered how gravity works?
options: *Sir Isaac Newton | Charles Darwin | Alexander Fleming | John Logie Baird
explanation: Sir Isaac Newton was born in Lincolnshire. His work on gravity and light changed the way people understood the world.

stem: What was the name of the new English Bible published during the reign of King James I?
options: *King James Bible | The Great Bible | The Latin Bible | The English Prayer Book
explanation: King James I asked for a new translation of the Bible into English. This version is still famous and used by many people today.

stem: Henry VIII had six wives. Which TWO of these wives were executed?
options: *Anne Boleyn | *Catherine Howard | Catherine of Aragon | Anne of Cleves
explanation: Both Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard were charged with being unfaithful to the King. They were executed at the Tower of London.

stem: In 1665, a terrible disease called the Great Plague killed thousands of people in London.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Great Plague was a serious illness that spread quickly in 1665. It was the last major outbreak of this disease in London.

stem: Which battle in Ireland was won by King William III in 1690?
options: *The Battle of the Boyne | The Battle of Hastings | The Battle of Bosworth | The Battle of Culloden
explanation: William III defeated the former king James II at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. This victory is still commemorated today in Northern Ireland.

stem: Which architect designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
options: *Sir Christopher Wren | Inigo Jones | Robert Adam | John Nash
explanation: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the old church burned down in 1666. It took over 30 years to build.

stem: Which monarch was invited back to rule when the monarchy was restored in 1660?
options: *Charles II | James II | William III | George I
explanation: Parliament invited Charles II to return from exile in 1660. This return of the royal family is known as the Restoration.

stem: Which English explorer was one of the first commanders to sail around the world?
options: *Sir Francis Drake | Captain James Cook | Sir Walter Raleigh | Horatio Nelson
explanation: Sir Francis Drake sailed around the world on his ship, the Golden Hind. He was also a leading commander against the Spanish Armada.

stem: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots, executed in 1587?
options: *She was suspected of plotting against Queen Elizabeth I | She refused to pay taxes to the English government | She led a French army to attack London | She surrendered Scotland to the Spanish king
explanation: Elizabeth I kept Mary in prison for nearly 20 years. Mary was executed because people believed she was plotting to take the English throne.

stem: What important rule did the Bill of Rights of 1689 establish?
options: *The monarch could not collect taxes without Parliament | Every adult citizen gained the right to vote | England and Scotland became separate nations | The monarch could appoint judges without approval
explanation: The Bill of Rights reduced royal power. It confirmed that the king or queen could not make laws or collect taxes without Parliament's consent.

stem: Who was the Spanish princess who became the first wife of King Henry VIII?
options: *Catherine of Aragon | Anne of Cleves | Catherine Parr | Kathryn Howard
explanation: Catherine of Aragon was Henry VIII's first wife and mother of Queen Mary I. Henry divorced her because she did not give him a male heir.

stem: During the reign of which king was Wales formally united with England?
options: *Henry VIII | Edward I | Henry VII | Charles I
explanation: Laws passed during the rule of Henry VIII united Wales with England and gave Welsh representatives seats in the English Parliament.

stem: Which 17th-century author wrote the famous epic poem Paradise Lost?
options: *John Milton | Geoffrey Chaucer | William Blake | Lord Byron
explanation: John Milton was a famous English writer during the Stuart period. He published Paradise Lost in 1667.

stem: In which year did Guy Fawkes and other plotters try to blow up Parliament?
explanation: The Gunpowder Plot took place in 1605. Catholics planned to blow up King James I and Parliament, but the plot was discovered in time.

stem: What nickname was given to people who fought for Parliament in the Civil War?
options: *Roundheads | Jacobites | Chartists | Suffragettes
explanation: Supporters of Parliament were called Roundheads because many cut their hair short. The king's supporters were called Cavaliers.

stem: Which TWO battles were fought during the English Civil War?
options: *The Battle of Marston Moor | *The Battle of Naseby | The Battle of Waterloo | The Battle of Trafalgar
explanation: Parliament's army won key victories against the king at Marston Moor in 1644 and Naseby in 1645. Waterloo and Trafalgar were fought much later.

stem: Which TWO monarchs belonged to the Tudor royal family?
options: *Henry VII | *Elizabeth I | James I | Charles II
explanation: Henry VII started the Tudor line in 1485, and Elizabeth I was the last Tudor ruler. James I and Charles II were from the House of Stuart.

stem: Queen Elizabeth I chose never to marry during her reign.
options: *True | False
explanation: Elizabeth I never married and was called the Virgin Queen. She ruled England successfully on her own for 45 years.

stem: Oliver Cromwell was crowned King of England after the Civil War ended.
options: True | *False
explanation: Cromwell was offered the crown but turned it down. He governed as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658.

stem: Which battle in 1485 ended the Wars of the Roses and put Henry VII on the throne?
options: Battle of Hastings | *Battle of Bosworth Field | Battle of Agincourt | Battle of Waterloo
explanation: Henry VII defeated Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485. This victory marked the start of the Tudor dynasty.

stem: Which of Henry VIII's wives survived him and lived after his death?
options: Anne of Cleves | *Catherine Parr | Catherine Howard | Jane Seymour
explanation: Catherine Parr was Henry VIII's sixth and final wife. She survived him when he died in 1547 and later married again.

stem: During the reign of King Edward VI, which book was written for use in the Church of England?
options: *The Book of Common Prayer | The King James Bible | The Pilgrim's Progress | The Canterbury Tales
explanation: The Book of Common Prayer was written during the reign of King Edward VI. It was created to help people worship in English rather than Latin.

stem: Which explorer sent people to establish the first English colonies in North America under Elizabeth I?
options: Sir Francis Drake | *Sir Walter Raleigh | Christopher Columbus | Henry Hudson
explanation: Sir Walter Raleigh was an explorer who tried to build English colonies in North America. He is also famous for bringing tobacco and potatoes to England.

stem: What did King Charles II do for the theatre when he came to the throne in 1660?
options: He banned all plays | *He let women act for the first time | He built the first theatre | He moved all theatres to Scotland
explanation: When Charles II became king in 1660, theatres were reopened after being banned by the Puritans. For the first time, women were allowed to perform as actors.

stem: Which emblem was created by Henry VII to show the union of the Houses of Lancaster and York?
options: The Red Dragon | *The Tudor Rose | The Golden Lion | The Thistle
explanation: King Henry VII created the Tudor Rose by joining the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York. This showed that the civil war had ended.

stem: Which famous group was set up during the reign of Charles II to promote science and natural knowledge?
options: *The Royal Society | The British Museum | The Royal Academy | The National Trust
explanation: The Royal Society was formed in 1660 to help scientists share and discuss their ideas. Famous members included Isaac Newton and Robert Boyle.

stem: What is the term for the belief that kings are chosen by God and do not have to answer to Parliament?
options: *The Divine Right of Kings | The Magna Carta | The Bill of Rights | The Great Charter
explanation: King James I and his son Charles I believed in the "Divine Right of Kings". This meant they thought only God could judge their actions, which angered Parliament.

stem: For how many years did King Charles I rule without calling Parliament at all?
options: 5 years | *11 years | 15 years | 20 years
explanation: King Charles I ruled without Parliament for 11 years. This period is often called the "Eleven Years' Tyranny" and helped lead to the Civil War.

stem: What name was given to the supporters of King James II who tried to rebel after he was removed from the throne?
options: *Jacobites | Roundheads | Suffragettes | Chartists
explanation: Supporters of James II were called Jacobites. They tried to return him or his heirs to the throne, leading to battles in Scotland and Ireland.

stem: Which TWO writers were famous playwrights during the Elizabethan era alongside William Shakespeare?
options: *Christopher Marlowe | *Ben Jonson | Geoffrey Chaucer | John Milton
explanation: Christopher Marlowe and Ben Jonson were both famous writers and playwrights during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, alongside William Shakespeare.

stem: Which TWO monarchs ruled England, Scotland and Ireland together after the Glorious Revolution?
options: *William III | *Mary II | James II | Anne
explanation: William III (William of Orange) and his wife Mary II ruled jointly. They were invited by Parliament to take the throne after James II fled to France.

stem: Queen Elizabeth I succeeded in keeping England as a Protestant country during her long reign.
options: *True | False
explanation: Elizabeth I made the Church of England Protestant again after the reign of her Catholic sister, Mary I. She did this while trying to avoid religious conflict.

stem: After the execution of King Charles I, England became a republic called the Commonwealth for eleven years.
options: *True | False
explanation: From 1649 to 1660, England had no monarch. It was a republic called the Commonwealth, governed mainly by Parliament and later by Oliver Cromwell.

stem: Which Stuart-era author wrote the highly popular religious book "The Pilgrim's Progress"?
options: *John Bunyan | John Milton | Daniel Defoe | Jonathan Swift
explanation: John Bunyan wrote "The Pilgrim's Progress" in 1678. It became one of the most famous and widely read books of the Stuart period.

stem: Who wrote a famous diary describing the Great Plague and the Great Fire of London?
options: *Samuel Pepys | Christopher Wren | William Shakespeare | John Milton
explanation: Samuel Pepys was a Member of Parliament who kept a detailed diary from 1660 to 1669. His diary is a famous account of the 1665 plague and the 1666 fire.

stem: In 1541, Henry VIII was the first English king to take which title?
options: *King of Ireland | King of Scotland | King of Wales | King of France
explanation: In 1541, Henry VIII took the title "King of Ireland". Previously, English monarchs had been known as the "Lord of Ireland".

stem: What was the main reason Henry VIII married his fourth wife, Anne of Cleves?
options: *For political reasons | Because he loved her | To unite with Scotland | She was his cousin
explanation: Henry VIII married Anne of Cleves to build a political link with German Protestants. He had the marriage cancelled soon after because he did not like her appearance.

stem: William of Orange was the ruler of which country before he became King of England?
options: *The Netherlands | France | Spain | Denmark
explanation: William of Orange was the ruler of the Netherlands. He was married to Mary, the daughter of King James II, and was invited to take the throne in 1688.

stem: Which TWO of these things did Scotland keep after joining with England in 1707?
options: *Its own legal system | *Its own Presbyterian Church | Its own Parliament | Its own monarch
explanation: While Scotland and England shared a monarch and parliament, Scotland kept its own legal and education systems. It also kept its own Presbyterian Church.

stem: Queen Elizabeth I's religious settlement followed a "middle way" to balance different Christian groups.
options: *True | False
explanation: Elizabeth I wanted to avoid religious conflict. Her settlement kept the Church of England Protestant, but it kept some Catholic-style traditions and ceremonies.

stem: Where is the Proms, an eight-week summer season of classical music, mainly held?
options: *The Royal Albert Hall | Wembley Stadium | The O2 Arena | Covent Garden
explanation: The Proms is a summer season of classical concerts held mainly at the Royal Albert Hall in London. It has run since 1895.

stem: Who composed 'Pomp and Circumstance'?
options: *Sir Edward Elgar | Benjamin Britten | Henry Purcell | Andrew Lloyd Webber
explanation: Sir Edward Elgar wrote the 'Pomp and Circumstance' marches. One is often sung as 'Land of Hope and Glory'.

stem: Who wrote Oliver Twist?
options: *Charles Dickens | Thomas Hardy | Jane Austen | Sir Arthur Conan Doyle
explanation: Charles Dickens wrote many famous novels, including Oliver Twist and Great Expectations. They show the lives of poor people in the 19th century.

stem: Who created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
options: *Sir Arthur Conan Doyle | Ian Fleming | Charles Dickens | Thomas Hardy
explanation: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor and writer, created Sherlock Holmes, one of the best-known fictional detectives.

stem: Which prize is given each year to a contemporary British artist?
options: *The Turner Prize | The Man Booker Prize | A BAFTA | The Laurence Olivier Award
explanation: The Turner Prize is named after the painter J M W Turner and celebrates contemporary art. The Man Booker Prize is for fiction.

stem: Who designed St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
options: *Sir Christopher Wren | Sir Edwin Lutyens | Capability Brown | Henry Moore
explanation: Sir Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's Cathedral and many London churches after the fire of 1666.

stem: The Eisteddfod is a Welsh festival of music, poetry and performance.
options: *True | False
explanation: The National Eisteddfod of Wales is a large festival of music, literature and performance, with many events in the Welsh language.

stem: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
options: *Jane Austen | Thomas Hardy | Charles Dickens | Agatha Christie
explanation: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility. Her novels are about marriage and family life.

stem: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in the 14th century?
options: *Geoffrey Chaucer | William Shakespeare | John Milton | Thomas Hardy
explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in the late 14th century. It is a famous collection of stories told by a group of pilgrims on their way to Canterbury.

stem: Which British composer wrote operas such as 'Dido and Aeneas' in the 17th century?
options: *Henry Purcell | Gustav Holst | Benjamin Britten | Edward Elgar
explanation: Henry Purcell was an organist at Westminster Abbey. He wrote church music, operas, and instrumental music that are still famous today.

stem: Which English landscape painter is famous for painting 'The Hay Wain'?
options: *John Constable | J.M.W. Turner | Thomas Gainsborough | David Hockney
explanation: John Constable was a famous landscape painter. 'The Hay Wain' is one of his most famous works, showing a rural scene in Suffolk, England.

stem: Which influential British film director made famous suspense films like 'The 39 Steps' and 'Psycho'?
options: *Alfred Hitchcock | David Lean | Ridley Scott | Danny Boyle
explanation: Alfred Hitchcock is widely regarded as one of the most influential filmmakers in cinema history. He was famous for his suspenseful thrillers.

stem: Who wrote the famous 20th-century novels 'Animal Farm' and 'Nineteen Eighty-Four'?
options: *George Orwell | Aldous Huxley | William Golding | Graham Greene
explanation: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Blair. He wrote 'Animal Farm' and 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', which are classic political novels.

stem: Which modern British architect designed the building known as 'The Gherkin' in London?
options: *Sir Norman Foster | Dame Zaha Hadid | Sir Edwin Lutyens | Inigo Jones
explanation: Sir Norman Foster is a leading modern architect who designed 'The Gherkin' in London, as well as the Millennium Bridge.

stem: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic operas in the 19th century, including 'The Mikado' and 'The Pirates of Penzance'.
options: *True | False
explanation: Gilbert and Sullivan wrote many famous comic operas in the 19th century. Their works are still regularly performed today.

stem: Which Scottish poet wrote 'Auld Lang Syne', a song traditionally sung on New Year's Eve?
options: *Robert Burns | Walter Scott | Lord Byron | Dylan Thomas
explanation: Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet. His poem 'Auld Lang Syne' is sung around the world to welcome the New Year.

stem: Which TWO of the following are famous plays written by William Shakespeare?
options: *Hamlet | *Romeo and Juliet | The Canterbury Tales | Paradise Lost
explanation: William Shakespeare wrote famous plays like 'Hamlet' and 'Romeo and Juliet' in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

stem: Which landscape artist is known as 'the painter of light' and has a major British art prize named after him?
options: *J.M.W. Turner | Joshua Reynolds | Henry Moore | L.S. Lowry
explanation: J.M.W. Turner was a highly influential artist famous for his paintings of water, light, and steam. The Turner Prize is named in his honour.

stem: Henry Moore was a famous British sculptor known for his large bronze abstract sculptures.
options: *True | False
explanation: Henry Moore was a highly influential sculptor who is especially known for his large bronze abstract sculptures of the human form.

stem: Who wrote 'Paradise Lost', an epic poem about the fall of mankind, published in 1667?
options: *John Milton | John Keats | William Wordsworth | Lord Tennyson
explanation: John Milton was a devout writer who wrote 'Paradise Lost', one of the most famous and influential epic poems in the English language.

stem: Which TWO of the following are famous British film awards or film festivals?
options: *The BAFTA Awards | *The London Film Festival | The Laurence Olivier Awards | The Mercury Prize
explanation: The BAFTA (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) awards are the UK's film industry awards. The London Film Festival is a major annual film event.

stem: Who is a famous British composer of musical theatre, known for writing 'Cats' and 'The Phantom of the Opera'?
options: *Andrew Lloyd Webber | Benjamin Britten | Ralph Vaughan Williams | Arthur Sullivan
explanation: Andrew Lloyd Webber has written some of the most successful musicals in history, which have been performed all over the world.

stem: Which of the Brontë sisters wrote the famous novel 'Wuthering Heights'?
options: *Emily Brontë | Charlotte Brontë | Anne Brontë | Maria Brontë
explanation: Emily Brontë wrote the gothic novel 'Wuthering Heights'. Her sister Charlotte wrote 'Jane Eyre'.

stem: Which of the Brontë sisters wrote the famous 1847 novel 'Jane Eyre'?
options: *Charlotte Brontë | Emily Brontë | Anne Brontë | Maria Brontë
explanation: Charlotte Brontë wrote the novel 'Jane Eyre' under the pen name Currer Bell. Her sister Emily wrote 'Wuthering Heights', and her sister Anne wrote 'Agnes Grey'.

stem: Which German-born composer became a British citizen and wrote the 'Messiah' in the 18th century?
options: *George Frideric Handel | Johann Sebastian Bach | Ludwig van Beethoven | Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
explanation: George Frideric Handel moved to London and became a British citizen. He is famous for 'Messiah' and 'Water Music', which was written for King George I.

stem: Which British fashion designer is famous for popularising the miniskirt in the 1960s?
options: *Mary Quant | Vivienne Westwood | Stella McCartney | Alexander McQueen
explanation: Mary Quant was a key figure in the fashion scene of the 1960s. She is widely credited with making the miniskirt popular with young women.

stem: Which British director is famous for directing epic films such as 'Lawrence of Arabia' and 'Doctor Zhivago'?
options: *David Lean | Alfred Hitchcock | Ridley Scott | Christopher Nolan
explanation: Sir David Lean was an acclaimed filmmaker who won Oscars for directing 'The Bridge on the River Kwai' and 'Lawrence of Arabia'.

stem: Which 18th-century artist is famous for his portraits, especially of people in country landscapes?
options: *Thomas Gainsborough | John Constable | J.M.W. Turner | L.S. Lowry
explanation: Thomas Gainsborough was a portrait and landscape painter. His works are known for their natural settings and elegant subjects.

stem: Which British architect designed the Cenotaph war memorial in Whitehall, London?
options: *Sir Edwin Lutyens | Sir Christopher Wren | Sir Norman Foster | Robert Adam
explanation: Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph, which is the site of the annual National Service of Remembrance. He also designed many buildings in New Delhi, India.

stem: Who wrote the famous 19th-century comedy play 'The Importance of Being Earnest'?
options: *Oscar Wilde | George Bernard Shaw | William Shakespeare | Harold Pinter
explanation: Oscar Wilde was an Irish writer and poet who wrote several popular plays in late-Victorian London, including 'The Importance of Being Earnest'.

stem: Which Scottish author wrote the classic adventure novels 'Treasure Island' and 'Kidnapped'?
options: *Robert Louis Stevenson | Sir Walter Scott | Arthur Conan Doyle | J.M. Barrie
explanation: Robert Louis Stevenson was a famous Scottish novelist and poet. He also wrote the classic thriller 'The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'.

stem: Which 20th-century British composer wrote 'The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra'?
options: *Benjamin Britten | Gustav Holst | Ralph Vaughan Williams | Edward Elgar
explanation: Benjamin Britten is one of the most famous British classical composers of the 20th century. He also founded the Aldeburgh Festival.

stem: Which famous English poet is closely associated with the Lake District and wrote a poem about daffodils?
options: *William Wordsworth | John Keats | Lord Byron | Wilfred Owen
explanation: William Wordsworth was a leader of the Romantic movement in English literature. He served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

stem: Which author wrote the famous fantasy novels 'The Hobbit' and 'The Lord of the Rings'?
options: *J.R.R. Tolkien | C.S. Lewis | Roald Dahl | George Orwell
explanation: J.R.R. Tolkien was an English writer and university professor. His books are among the best-selling fantasy novels of all time.

stem: Which TWO of the following are famous annual music festivals in the UK?
options: *Glastonbury | *Glyndebourne | Wimbledon | Royal Ascot
explanation: Glastonbury is a famous pop and rock music festival held in Somerset. Glyndebourne is a world-famous festival of opera held in Sussex.

stem: Which TWO of the following novels were written by Charles Dickens?
options: *Great Expectations | *David Copperfield | Pride and Prejudice | Jane Eyre
explanation: Charles Dickens was a famous Victorian writer. Some of his most popular novels include 'Great Expectations', 'David Copperfield', and 'A Christmas Carol'.

stem: Sir Walter Scott was a famous Scottish writer who wrote historical novels and poems.
options: *True | False
explanation: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish writer of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. His famous works include 'Waverley' and 'Rob Roy'.

stem: The Mercury Prize is awarded every year for the best music album from the UK and Ireland.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Mercury Prize is a prestigious annual music award. It is given for the best music album of the year by a British or Irish artist.

stem: When is Boxing Day?
options: *26 December | 24 December | 1 January | 31 December
explanation: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day, 26 December. It is a public holiday.

stem: What is New Year's Eve called in Scotland?
options: *Hogmanay | Burns Night | Ceilidh | Eisteddfod
explanation: In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay. For some Scottish people it is a bigger celebration than Christmas.

stem: What do people remember on Bonfire Night, 5 November?
options: *A failed plot to blow up Parliament in 1605 | The end of the First World War | The Battle of Hastings | The Great Fire of London
explanation: In 1605 a group of Catholics, including Guy Fawkes, tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament. People mark this with fireworks and bonfires.

stem: Why do many people wear poppies in early November?
options: *To remember people who died in wars | To celebrate the harvest | To mark the start of winter | To celebrate Guy Fawkes
explanation: Remembrance Day is 11 November. People wear red poppies to remember those who died fighting for the UK and its allies.

stem: When is Valentine's Day?
options: *14 February | 1 April | 14 March | 31 October
explanation: On Valentine's Day, 14 February, people send cards or gifts to someone they love.

stem: On 1 April, people traditionally play jokes on each other until midday.
options: *True | False
explanation: April Fool's Day is on 1 April. People play jokes on each other, but only until midday.

stem: Which TWO of these are Christian festivals?
options: *Easter | *Christmas | Diwali | Hanukkah
explanation: Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus and Easter remembers his death and resurrection. Diwali is a Hindu and Sikh festival and Hanukkah is Jewish.

stem: On which date is Halloween?
options: *31 October | 1 November | 5 November | 11 November
explanation: Halloween is on 31 October. Children often dress up and go 'trick or treating'.

stem: When is Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) celebrated in the UK?
options: 14 February | *Three weeks before Easter | 25 December | The first Sunday in May
explanation: Mothering Sunday is held three weeks before Easter. It is a traditional day to honor mothers and often involves giving cards or flowers.

stem: On which day is St Patrick's Day celebrated?
options: 1 March | *17 March | 23 April | 30 November
explanation: St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland. His feast day is 17 March and it is a public holiday in Northern Ireland.

stem: Which religious festival marks the end of Ramadan, the month of fasting?
options: Eid al-Adha | *Eid al-Fitr | Diwali | Vaisakhi
explanation: Eid al-Fitr is a Muslim festival that celebrates the end of fasting. People often enjoy special meals and give to charity during this time.

stem: What is often called the 'Festival of Lights' and is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs?
options: *Diwali | Hanukkah | Vaisakhi | Easter
explanation: Diwali is a major festival for Hindus and Sikhs. It celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil.

stem: Which TWO of these statements about bank holidays are correct?
options: They fall on the same dates every year | *Most businesses and banks close | Everyone in the UK must have the day off | *There are several bank holidays every year
explanation: Bank holidays are public holidays when most banks and businesses close. They are held at different times, such as in the spring and late summer.

stem: What is a 'pantomime' in British tradition?
options: A serious opera | *A comedy play based on a fairy tale | A type of classical dance | A formal dinner party
explanation: Pantomimes are funny plays traditionally performed at Christmas. They are often based on well-known fairy tales and involve audience participation.

stem: Roast turkey is a traditional food for Christmas dinner in the UK.
options: *True | False
explanation: Many people in the UK eat roast turkey for their main Christmas meal. Other traditional items include Christmas pudding and mince pies.

stem: Which tradition was popularized in the UK by Queen Victoria's husband, Prince Albert?
options: Giving chocolate eggs | *Putting up a Christmas tree | Playing jokes on April 1st | Wearing poppies
explanation: Prince Albert brought the tradition of the Christmas tree to the UK from Germany. It became a common custom during the 19th century.

stem: Which religious group celebrates Vaisakhi to remember the founding of the Khalsa?
options: Jews | Muslims | *Sikhs | Buddhists
explanation: Vaisakhi is an important Sikh festival. It celebrates the founding of the Khalsa (the community of initiated Sikhs) by Guru Gobind Singh.

stem: Hanukkah is a Jewish festival that lasts for eight days.
options: *True | False
explanation: Hanukkah is the Jewish Festival of Lights. It lasts for eight days and remembers the miracle of the oil in the Temple.

stem: What does the Christian festival of Good Friday commemorate?
options: The birth of Jesus | *The death of Jesus | The resurrection of Jesus | The arrival of the Wise Men
explanation: Good Friday marks the day Jesus Christ died on the cross. It is followed by Easter Sunday, which celebrates his return to life.

stem: When is Father's Day celebrated in the UK?
options: The first Sunday in March | *The third Sunday in June | The last Sunday in August | The second Sunday in November
explanation: Father's Day is a day to celebrate fathers and father figures. It is held on the third Sunday in June.

stem: Which TWO things are traditionally associated with Easter in the UK?
options: Carving pumpkins | *Giving chocolate eggs | *Eating hot cross buns | Lighting fireworks
explanation: People often give chocolate eggs at Easter to represent new life. Hot cross buns, which are sweet breads with a cross on top, are also a traditional food.

stem: Lent is the period of 40 days before Easter when some people give up certain foods.
options: *True | False
explanation: Lent is a time of reflection and fasting in the Christian calendar. It lasts for 40 days leading up to the celebration of Easter.

stem: In Scotland, what is the tradition of 'first footing' on New Year's Day?
options: Running a race | *Being the first guest to enter a home | Cooking a large breakfast | Singing songs in the street
explanation: First footing is a Scottish tradition where the first person to visit a home in the New Year brings gifts like coal to bring luck.

stem: When is St Andrew's Day, the national day of Scotland?
options: *30 November | 1 March | 23 April | 17 March
explanation: St Andrew's Day is celebrated on 30 November. It is Scotland's national day and is a bank holiday there.

stem: Which of these is the holiest day of the year in Judaism, marked by a 25-hour period of fasting?
options: *Yom Kippur | Rosh Hashanah | Hanukkah | Purim
explanation: Yom Kippur is the holiest day of the Jewish year. It is a day of fasting and prayer when Jewish people ask for forgiveness.

stem: Which religious festival is celebrated by Buddhists to remember the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha?
options: *Wesak | Diwali | Vaisakhi | Eid
explanation: Wesak is an important festival for Buddhists. It takes place in May and is a time for people to visit temples and give gifts.

stem: What sweet, fruit-filled pies are traditionally eaten at Christmas in the UK?
options: *Mince pies | Apple pies | Pecan pies | Pumpkin pies
explanation: Mince pies are small, sweet pastries filled with dried fruits and spices. They are a popular food during the Christmas season in the UK.

stem: On what date is Remembrance Day, which commemorates those who died in wars?
options: *11 November | 5 November | 25 December | 1 January
explanation: Remembrance Day is on 11 November. At 11:00 am, people observe a two-minute silence to remember those who died fighting for their country.

stem: Who makes a traditional television and radio broadcast to the nation on Christmas Day?
options: *The Monarch | The Prime Minister | The Archbishop of Canterbury | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The Monarch (the King or Queen) makes a speech to the UK and the Commonwealth on Christmas Day. This tradition was started by King George V in 1932.

stem: What is the historical origin of the name 'Boxing Day'?
options: *Giving small boxes of gifts or money to workers | A traditional sport played on the day after Christmas | Packing up Christmas decorations into cardboard boxes | The royal family collecting charity boxes from the public
explanation: Boxing Day, on 26 December, traditionally got its name from the practice of giving small boxes of money or food to servants and tradespeople.

stem: What is the British tradition of making a promise to behave better or stop a bad habit in the new year called?
options: *New Year's resolution | New Year's wish | New Year's toast | New Year's choice
explanation: A New Year's resolution is a promise that people make to improve their lives starting on 1 January. Common resolutions include eating healthier or exercising more.

stem: Northern Ireland has more bank holidays than England and Wales.
options: *True | False
explanation: Northern Ireland has ten bank holidays a year, while England and Wales have eight. Scotland has nine bank holidays.

stem: Ash Wednesday marks the beginning of the Christian period known as Lent.
options: *True | False
explanation: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, which is a 40-day period of fasting and prayer before Easter.

stem: Which TWO of the following are Jewish festivals?
options: *Rosh Hashanah | *Yom Kippur | Wesak | Diwali
explanation: Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) and Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) are two major festivals in Judaism. Wesak is Buddhist and Diwali is Hindu.

stem: Which TWO of these dates are bank holidays in all parts of the UK?
options: *Christmas Day | *New Year's Day | St George's Day | St David's Day
explanation: Christmas Day and New Year's Day are official bank holidays in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. National saint days are not bank holidays in all parts of the UK.

stem: Which food is traditionally from Scotland?
options: *Haggis | Yorkshire pudding | Welsh cakes | Ulster fry
explanation: Haggis is a traditional Scottish dish made from sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, oats and spices. It is often eaten on Burns Night.

stem: Which dish is traditionally linked to England?
options: *Roast beef with Yorkshire pudding | Haggis | Welsh cakes | Ulster fry
explanation: Roast beef, often served with Yorkshire pudding made from batter, is a traditional English meal.

stem: You need a TV licence to watch programmes on any device at the time they are broadcast.
options: *True | False
explanation: A TV licence is needed to watch or record live TV on any device, including a computer or phone. The money helps pay for the BBC.

stem: What are national parks?
options: *Protected areas of countryside that everyone can visit | Gardens owned by the monarch | Sports grounds for local teams | Private estates that are closed to visitors
explanation: National parks are areas of protected countryside. They are open to everyone for walking, camping and other activities.

stem: What is 'Laverbread', a traditional food from Wales?
options: *A type of seaweed | A spicy meat pie | A fruit cake | A local cheese
explanation: Laverbread is a traditional Welsh dish made from seaweed. It is often fried with oatmeal and served with bacon for breakfast.

stem: In England and Wales, how long can large shops open for on a Sunday?
options: *Up to six hours | Up to ten hours | Up to twelve hours | They must stay closed
explanation: In England and Wales, large shops (over 280 square metres) can only open for a maximum of six hours on Sundays. Small shops have no opening time limits.

stem: The National Trust is a charity that works to protect historic houses and nature.
options: *True | False
explanation: The National Trust was founded in 1895. It has more than four million members and looks after many historic buildings and natural areas across the UK.

stem: Which TWO of the following rock bands became famous in the 1960s and 1970s?
options: *The Rolling Stones | *The Who | The Beach Boys | ABBA
explanation: The Rolling Stones and The Who are two of the most famous rock bands in history. They became world-famous during the 1960s and continue to be popular.

stem: Where was the popular dish 'Chicken Tikka Masala' first created?
options: *In the United Kingdom | In India | In Pakistan | In Bangladesh
explanation: Chicken Tikka Masala is an Indian-style dish that was actually invented in the UK. It is now considered one of the most popular meals in the country.

stem: Which BBC radio station is mostly for a younger audience and plays pop music?
options: *Radio 1 | Radio 2 | Radio 3 | Radio 4
explanation: BBC Radio 1 plays modern pop and rock music and is aimed at younger listeners. Radio 3 is known for classical music and Radio 4 for news and talk.

stem: The artist David Hockney is famous for which type of modern art?
options: *Pop art | Abstract sculpture | Wood carving | Black and white photography
explanation: David Hockney was an important part of the 1960s pop art movement. He remains one of the most influential and popular British artists of the modern era.

stem: Which of these is one of the most popular hobbies in the UK?
options: *Gardening | Skydiving | Deep-sea fishing | Mountain climbing
explanation: Gardening is a very popular hobby in the UK. Many people who do not have their own garden can rent a small piece of land called an allotment.

stem: Which TWO of the following are the largest youth organisations in the UK?
options: *The Scout Association | *Girlguiding | The Cadet Force | The Youth Hostel Association
explanation: The Scout Association and Girlguiding UK are the two largest youth groups in the UK. They help young people learn new skills and participate in outdoor activities.

stem: Which artist is famous for creating works that use animals preserved in chemicals?
options: *Damien Hirst | Henry Moore | David Hockney | John Constable
explanation: Damien Hirst is a leading member of the 'Young British Artists' group. He is famous for work that includes animals preserved in liquid.

stem: On which day of the week do many shops in town centres stay open late?
options: *Thursday | Monday | Wednesday | Friday
explanation: Many shops in town centres stay open later than usual on Thursday evenings. This is often called 'late-night shopping'.

stem: Volunteering is when people work for no pay to help their local community.
options: *True | False
explanation: Volunteering is a great way to help the community and meet new people. Many charities and groups in the UK rely on volunteers to do their work.

stem: What name is given to large cinemas that have many screens showing different films?
options: *Multiplexes | Art houses | Studios | Stages
explanation: Most towns and cities in the UK have a large cinema called a multiplex. These buildings have several screens showing many different films at the same time.

stem: In which part of London is the National Gallery located?
options: *Trafalgar Square | Piccadilly Circus | Hyde Park | Covent Garden
explanation: The National Gallery is a famous art museum in Trafalgar Square, London. It houses a collection of more than 2,000 Western European paintings.

stem: Which city hosts the largest arts festival in the world every summer?
options: *Edinburgh | Cardiff | Belfast | London
explanation: The Edinburgh Festival is held every August in Scotland's capital. It is the largest arts festival in the world and includes many theatre and comedy shows.

stem: Which part of England is famous for the 'Cornish Pasty', which is a pastry filled with meat and vegetables?
options: *Cornwall | Yorkshire | Kent | Norfolk
explanation: The Cornish Pasty comes from Cornwall in the South West of England. It was originally made as a portable meal for miners to take to work.

stem: Which area in London is world-famous for its many theatres and musical shows?
options: *The West End | The East End | The City | The Docklands
explanation: The West End is the centre of the theatre industry in London. Many world-famous musicals and plays have been running there for decades.

stem: Which TWO of the following are examples of traditional British desserts or puddings?
options: *Apple crumble | *Bread and butter pudding | Crepes | Gelato
explanation: Apple crumble and bread and butter pudding are classic British desserts. They are often served with custard, which is a sweet, yellow sauce.

stem: Many people in the UK rent a small piece of land called an 'allotment' to grow their own fruit and vegetables.
options: *True | False
explanation: Allotments are popular with people who do not have a garden at home. They are a great way to spend time outdoors and grow fresh food.

stem: Which of these is a traditional British meal of tea, sandwiches, and small cakes often served in the late afternoon?
options: *Afternoon tea | Brunch | Supper | High lunch
explanation: Afternoon tea is a famous British tradition. It usually includes scones with jam and cream, along with a selection of finger sandwiches.

stem: Which of these is a famous type of cheese that was first made in a village in Somerset, England?
options: *Cheddar | Camembert | Brie | Edam
explanation: Cheddar is the most popular type of cheese in the UK. It was originally made in the village of Cheddar in the county of Somerset.

stem: What is Big Ben?
options: *The great bell in the clock at the Houses of Parliament | The tower of Westminster Abbey | A large clock in Trafalgar Square | The main bell of St Paul's Cathedral
explanation: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell in the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament. The tower was named Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

stem: In which county is the Eden Project, with its huge greenhouses of plants?
options: *Cornwall | Devon | Kent | Somerset
explanation: The Eden Project in Cornwall has large domes holding plants from around the world. It is also an educational charity.

stem: Where is the Giant's Causeway?
options: *Northern Ireland | Scotland | Wales | England
explanation: The Giant's Causeway is on the north-east coast of Northern Ireland. It is made of thousands of six-sided rock columns.

stem: Which national park contains Windermere, the largest lake in England?
options: *The Lake District | Snowdonia | The Peak District | Dartmoor
explanation: The Lake District is England's largest national park. Windermere is England's largest lake.

stem: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
options: *Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) | Ben Nevis | Scafell Pike | Slieve Donard
explanation: Snowdon, also called Yr Wyddfa, is the highest mountain in Wales. Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest in the UK.

stem: Loch Lomond, the largest area of fresh water in mainland Britain, is in which country?
options: *Scotland | Wales | England | Northern Ireland
explanation: Loch Lomond is in Scotland. It is part of the Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.

stem: The London Eye is a large observation wheel on the south bank of the River Thames.
options: *True | False
explanation: The London Eye opened to mark the year 2000. From the top, visitors can see across much of London.

stem: Where is the famous prehistoric monument Stonehenge located?
options: *Wiltshire | Cornwall | Yorkshire | Cumbria
explanation: Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument located in the English county of Wiltshire. It was built in stages starting about 5,000 years ago.

stem: Which famous building in London was started by William the Conqueror and now keeps the Crown Jewels?
options: *The Tower of London | Westminster Abbey | The Houses of Parliament | Kensington Palace
explanation: The Tower of London was built by William the Conqueror after 1066. Today, visitors can see the Crown Jewels kept there.

stem: Who built the stone wall in the north of England to keep out tribes from Scotland?
options: *The Romans | The Normans | The Anglo-Saxons | The Victorians
explanation: The Roman Emperor Hadrian ordered the wall to be built in AD 122. Parts of Hadrian's Wall are still standing today.

stem: What was the first national park to be established in the UK?
options: *The Peak District | The Lake District | Snowdonia | The Yorkshire Dales
explanation: The Peak District, located mainly in Derbyshire, was designated as the UK's first national park in 1951. It is famous for its dales and hills.

stem: Which historic fortress dominates the skyline of Scotland's capital city?
options: *Edinburgh Castle | Stirling Castle | Urquhart Castle | Balmoral Castle
explanation: Edinburgh Castle is built on an extinct volcano and dominates the city. It has played a key role in Scottish military history.

stem: What is the popular name for the Parliament Buildings in Belfast, Northern Ireland?
options: *Stormont | The Guildhall | The Holywood | Clifton House
explanation: Stormont is the home of the Northern Ireland Assembly. It is located in a large park in the east of Belfast.

stem: In which country of the UK is the Snowdonia National Park located?
options: *Wales | Scotland | England | Northern Ireland
explanation: Snowdonia is a national park in north Wales. It is famous for its high mountains and deep valleys.

stem: Which famous Welsh castle, built by Edward I, is a World Heritage Site?
options: *Caernarfon Castle | Cardiff Castle | Windsor Castle | Edinburgh Castle
explanation: Edward I built Caernarfon Castle in north Wales in the late 13th century. It is famous for its unique polygonal towers.

stem: Where have British monarchs been crowned since the year 1066?
options: *Westminster Abbey | St Paul's Cathedral | Canterbury Cathedral | Windsor Castle
explanation: Westminster Abbey in London is the traditional place of coronation for British monarchs. Many famous historical figures are also buried there.

stem: What is Scotland's first national park, which contains a very large freshwater loch?
options: *Loch Lomond and The Trossachs | The Cairngorms | Lake District | Snowdonia
explanation: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs was created as Scotland's first national park in 2002. It is located in the west of the country.

stem: Which castle is famous for being the oldest and largest occupied castle in the world?
options: *Windsor Castle | Edinburgh Castle | Warwick Castle | Dover Castle
explanation: Windsor Castle has been a royal residence for over 900 years. It is located just outside London.

stem: Which TWO of the following are famous gardens located in the UK?
options: *Bodnant Garden in Wales | *Mount Stewart in Northern Ireland | Central Park | Versailles Gardens
explanation: Bodnant Garden in Wales is famous for its plants, and Mount Stewart in Northern Ireland has beautiful formal gardens.

stem: Which TWO of the following are famous tourist sights in Northern Ireland?
options: *The Belfast City Hall | *The Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge | Hadrian's Wall | The Peak District
explanation: Belfast City Hall was built in 1906, and the rope bridge connects the mainland to a tiny island. Both are popular sights in Northern Ireland.

stem: The city of Derry/Londonderry in Northern Ireland is famous for having complete, unbroken stone walls around its old city.
options: *True | False
explanation: Derry/Londonderry is the only remaining completely walled city in Ireland. The walls were built in the 17th century.

stem: Which country of the UK contains the Cairngorms National Park, the largest national park in the country?
options: *Scotland | England | Wales | Northern Ireland
explanation: The Cairngorms National Park is in Scotland. It is the largest national park in the UK and has spectacular mountains and forests.

stem: Which famous British prime minister was born at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire?
options: *Sir Winston Churchill | Clement Attlee | Margaret Thatcher | Harold Wilson
explanation: Sir Winston Churchill was born at Blenheim Palace. It is a large country house built in the early 18th century and is a World Heritage Site.

stem: Which national park in Wales is famous for being the only one in the UK focused mainly on a coastal landscape?
options: *Pembrokeshire Coast | Snowdonia | Brecon Beacons | Peak District
explanation: The Pembrokeshire Coast National Park is in southwest Wales. It was established in 1952 and has beautiful cliffs, beaches and wildlife.

stem: In which English city can you visit the famous ancient baths built by the Romans around natural hot springs?
options: *Bath | York | Canterbury | Chester
explanation: The Roman Baths are located in the city of Bath in Somerset. The Romans built a temple and bathing complex there over 2,000 years ago.

stem: The Lake District is the largest national park in England.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Lake District is the largest national park in England, covering over 2,300 square kilometres. It is famous for its beautiful lakes and fells.

stem: Which TWO of the following are major national museums in the UK?
options: *British Museum | *National Museum Cardiff | Louvre Museum | Prado Museum
explanation: The British Museum in London and the National Museum Cardiff in Wales are major national museums. They hold world-famous collections of art and history.

stem: Which large loch in Scotland is famous for the legendary monster that is said to live in its deep water?
options: *Loch Ness | Loch Lomond | Loch Katrine | Loch Tay
explanation: Loch Ness is a large, deep freshwater loch in the Scottish Highlands. It is world-famous because of the legend of the Loch Ness Monster, often called 'Nessie'.

stem: What is the name of the historic outdoor theatre in London, rebuilt near its original site, where Shakespeare's plays are performed?
options: *Shakespeare's Globe | The Royal Opera House | The National Theatre | The London Coliseum
explanation: Shakespeare's Globe is a modern reconstruction of the original globe-shaped outdoor theatre built in 1599. It stands on the south bank of the River Thames.

stem: The Forth Bridge is a famous red railway bridge that spans the Firth of Forth in Scotland.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Forth Bridge is a world-famous cantilever railway bridge opened in 1890. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site located near Edinburgh.

stem: Which historic castle, located in the center of the Welsh capital city, has walls that date back to Roman times?
options: *Cardiff Castle | Edinburgh Castle | Windsor Castle | Caernarfon Castle
explanation: Cardiff Castle is located in the heart of Cardiff, the capital city of Wales. It has a rich history, with Roman forts, a Norman keep and Victorian decoration.

stem: In which part of the UK are the Mourne Mountains located?
options: *Northern Ireland | Scotland | Wales | England
explanation: The Mourne Mountains are in Northern Ireland. They are known for their beautiful granite peaks and inspired the famous writer C.S. Lewis.

stem: Which TWO of the following historic locations are located in London?
options: *Westminster Abbey | *The Tower of London | Edinburgh Castle | Stormont
explanation: Both Westminster Abbey and the Tower of London are located in London. Edinburgh Castle is in Scotland and Stormont is in Northern Ireland.

stem: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
options: *St Andrew | St David | St George | St Patrick
explanation: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland and St Andrew's Day is 30 November. St David is for Wales, St George for England and St Patrick for Northern Ireland.

stem: When is St David's Day, the national day of Wales?
options: *1 March | 17 March | 23 April | 30 November
explanation: St David's Day is on 1 March. St Patrick's Day is 17 March, St George's Day is 23 April and St Andrew's Day is 30 November.

stem: When is St George's Day?
options: *23 April | 1 March | 17 March | 30 November
explanation: St George is the patron saint of England and his day is 23 April.

stem: Who is the head of the Church of England?
options: *The monarch | The Archbishop of Canterbury | The Prime Minister | The Pope
explanation: The monarch is the head of the Church of England. The Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader.

stem: People in the UK are free to choose any religion, or to have no religion.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK has religious freedom. People can follow any faith, change their faith or have none.

stem: What is the national church in Scotland?
options: *The Church of Scotland | The Church of England | The Church in Wales | The Roman Catholic Church
explanation: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church. It is run by ministers and elders, not by the monarch.

stem: Which Christian group is governed by a General Assembly and a Moderator?
options: The Church of England | *The Church of Scotland | The Roman Catholic Church | The Methodist Church
explanation: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church. It is led by the Moderator of the General Assembly, who serves for one year.

stem: The Church in Wales and the Church of Ireland are 'established' churches like the Church of England.
options: True | *False
explanation: Only the Church of England and the Church of Scotland are established churches. This means they have a special legal link with the state.

stem: Who was the founder of the Methodist Church in the 18th century?
options: George Fox | *John Wesley | William Booth | Thomas Cranmer
explanation: John Wesley founded the Methodist Church to reach people who did not attend the Church of England. It is now one of the largest 'Free Churches' in the UK.

stem: Which religious group is also known as the 'Religious Society of Friends'?
options: The Salvation Army | *The Quakers | The Baptists | The Methodists
explanation: The Quakers were founded by George Fox in the 17th century. They are known for their commitment to peace and simple living.

stem: Which TWO of the following are examples of 'Free Churches' in the UK?
options: *Methodist Church | Church of England | *Baptist Church | Roman Catholic Church
explanation: Free Churches are Christian groups that are not part of the established Church of England. Other examples include the United Reformed Church.

stem: Who started the Salvation Army in the 19th century to help the poor?
options: John Wesley | *William and Catherine Booth | George Fox | The Pope
explanation: The Salvation Army is a Christian group that focuses on social work. It works in many countries to provide food and shelter to people in need.

stem: The United Kingdom is a secular society, which means that religious ideas do not govern the laws of the country.
options: *True | False
explanation: Although there are established churches, the UK is a secular society. This means everyone is free to practice any religion or none at all.

stem: What is another name for the Church of England?
options: The Presbyterian Church | *The Anglican Church | The Catholic Church | The Orthodox Church
explanation: The Church of England is often called the Anglican Church. In other countries, churches with similar beliefs are part of the Anglican Communion.

stem: How long does the Moderator of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland serve for?
options: *One year | Five years | Ten years | For life
explanation: The Moderator is the head of the Church of Scotland for a 12-month period. They represent the church at official events.

stem: Which religious leader is the spiritual head of the Roman Catholic Church?
options: The Archbishop of Canterbury | The Moderator | *The Pope | The Chief Rabbi
explanation: The Roman Catholic Church has millions of members in the UK. Its worldwide leader is the Pope, who is based in the Vatican.

stem: Which TWO of the following statements about the Church of England are true?
options: *It is the established church in England. | *The Monarch is the head of the church. | It is a Presbyterian church. | It has no links to the state.
explanation: The Church of England was established during the Reformation. The King or Queen holds the title 'Defender of the Faith' as its head.

stem: People in the UK are allowed to change their religion at any time.
options: *True | False
explanation: Freedom of religion is a key part of life in the UK. People can choose their own faith, change it, or have no religion at all.

stem: Which church in the UK is a Presbyterian church?
options: The Church of England | *The Church of Scotland | The Roman Catholic Church | The Methodist Church
explanation: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church, which means it is governed by elders. It is one of the two established churches in the UK.

stem: Who has the right to appoint the Archbishop of Canterbury?
options: The Pope | The Prime Minister | *The Monarch | The General Assembly
explanation: The Monarch is the head of the Church of England. They appoint senior church leaders on the advice of the Prime Minister.

stem: Which Christian group grew quickly in the 18th century by preaching in the streets to working people?
options: The Quakers | *The Methodists | The Roman Catholics | The Baptists
explanation: Methodism began as a movement within the Church of England. John Wesley and others travelled around the country to reach people who did not go to church.

stem: How many senior bishops of the Church of England sit in the House of Lords?
explanation: There are 26 senior Church of England bishops who have seats in the House of Lords. This shows the church's role as the official state religion in England.

stem: The British monarch has the official title ‘Defender of the Faith’.
options: *True | False
explanation: The monarch is the head of the Church of England and uses the title 'Defender of the Faith'. This title has been used by monarchs for hundreds of years.

stem: In the UK census, which of these is the largest religious group after Christians?
options: *Muslims | Hindus | Sikhs | Buddhists
explanation: According to census data, Islam is the second largest religion in the UK. There are also many people who say they have no religion at all.

stem: Which TWO of these major religions have many followers in the UK today?
options: *Hinduism | *Judaism | Shintoism | Taoism
explanation: The UK is home to people from many faiths. Hinduism and Judaism are two of the largest non-Christian religious groups in the country.

stem: Which of these statements about the monarch and the Church of Scotland is true?
options: *The monarch is a member but not the head | The monarch is the supreme governor | The monarch chooses the church leaders | The monarch is not allowed to join
explanation: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church and is independent. The monarch is a member of the church but does not lead it.

stem: Where is the Grand National horse race held?
options: *Aintree, near Liverpool | Ascot | Epsom | Newmarket
explanation: The Grand National is a famous horse race at Aintree, near Liverpool. Royal Ascot is another well-known race meeting.

stem: Which is the oldest tennis tournament in the world?
options: *Wimbledon | The US Open | The French Open | The Australian Open
explanation: The Wimbledon Championships began in 1877. It is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only major one played on grass.

stem: Which town in Scotland is known as the home of golf?
options: *St Andrews | Gleneagles | Inverness | Stirling
explanation: Golf has been played in Scotland since the 15th century. St Andrews is known around the world as the home of golf.

stem: Who was the first man to run a mile in under four minutes, in 1954?
options: *Sir Roger Bannister | Sir Steve Redgrave | Sir Chris Hoy | Sir Mo Farah
explanation: Sir Roger Bannister ran a mile in under four minutes in 1954. Nobody had done it before.

stem: How many times had London hosted the Olympic Games by 2012?
options: *Three | Two | One | Four
explanation: London hosted the Olympic Games in 1908, 1948 and 2012. The 2012 Games were held mainly in Stratford, east London.

stem: The Paralympic Games began from work at which hospital?
options: *Stoke Mandeville | Great Ormond Street | St Thomas' | Addenbrooke's
explanation: Sport for disabled people was developed at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Buckinghamshire. This work led to the Paralympic Games.

stem: Sir Steve Redgrave won rowing gold medals at five Olympic Games in a row.
options: *True | False
explanation: Sir Steve Redgrave won gold in rowing at five Olympic Games one after another, from 1984 to 2000.

stem: In which sport do England and Australia compete for The Ashes?
options: *Cricket | Rugby | Tennis | Golf
explanation: The Ashes is a famous series of cricket matches between England and Australia.

stem: Which golf tournament is a famous competition played between teams from Europe and the United States?
options: *The Ryder Cup | The Walker Cup | The Open Championship | The Masters
explanation: The Ryder Cup is held every two years. It is played between teams of male golfers from Europe and the United States.

stem: Which country won the FIFA World Cup when it was hosted in England in 1966?
options: *England | Germany | Brazil | Scotland
explanation: England won the football World Cup in 1966 on home soil. This remains England's only World Cup victory so far.

stem: Which TWO of the following are the main types of rugby played in the UK, each having different rules?
options: *Rugby Union | *Rugby League | Rugby Association | Rugby National
explanation: Rugby Union and Rugby League are the two main types of rugby. They have different rules, including the number of players in a team.

stem: Who was the first cyclist from the UK to win the famous Tour de France race?
options: *Sir Bradley Wiggins | Sir Chris Hoy | Mark Cavendish | Geraint Thomas
explanation: Sir Bradley Wiggins won the Tour de France in 2012. He also won several Olympic gold medals in cycling during his career.

stem: Dame Ellen MacArthur is famous for her achievements in which of the following sports?
options: *Sailing | Rowing | Swimming | Athletics
