explanation: In 2005, Dame Ellen MacArthur became the fastest person to sail around the world solo.

stem: Which of these is a famous flat horse race held at Epsom in Surrey since 1780?
options: *The Derby | The Oaks | The St Leger | The Royal Stakes
explanation: The Epsom Derby is a very famous flat horse race. It is held annually in June and has been run since 1780.

stem: In cricket, the longest matches are called Test matches and can last for up to five days.
options: *True | False
explanation: Test matches are the traditional form of cricket. They can last for up to five days and can still end in a draw.

stem: Sir Jackie Stewart is a famous Scottish sportsman who won three world championships in which sport?
options: *Formula 1 motor racing | Snooker | Golf | Darts
explanation: Sir Jackie Stewart was a highly successful Formula 1 driver. He won three World Championships during his career.

stem: Dame Kelly Holmes won two gold medals at the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens in which sport?
options: *Athletics | Swimming | Sailing | Gymnastics
explanation: Dame Kelly Holmes won Olympic gold in both the 800 metres and 1,500 metres middle-distance running events.

stem: Which TWO of the following European countries play in the annual Six Nations rugby union championship?
options: *France | *Italy | Germany | Spain
explanation: The Six Nations championship is played by England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy.

stem: Sir Chris Hoy is one of the UK's most successful Olympians, winning six gold medals in which sport?
options: *Track cycling | Rowing | Sailing | Swimming
explanation: Sir Chris Hoy is a Scottish track cyclist. He won six Olympic gold medals and eleven world championship titles.

stem: Royal Ascot is a famous five-day horse racing event attended by members of the Royal Family.
options: *True | False
explanation: Royal Ascot is held in Berkshire every year. It is famous for its high fashion and is traditionally attended by the Royal Family.

stem: Under what name do athletes from Great Britain and Northern Ireland compete together in the Olympic Games?
options: *Great Britain | United Kingdom | British Isles | The Royal Team
explanation: Athletics and sports teams from Great Britain and Northern Ireland compete together as Great Britain (often called Team GB).

stem: Where is the British Grand Prix, a famous Formula 1 motor race, held every year?
options: *Silverstone | Brands Hatch | Donington Park | Ascot
explanation: The British Grand Prix is a major Formula 1 event held annually at Silverstone in Northamptonshire. Motor racing has a long history in the UK.

stem: Which two universities compete in the famous annual boat race on the River Thames?
options: *Oxford and Cambridge | London and Bristol | Edinburgh and Glasgow | Durham and York
explanation: The Boat Race is an annual rowing race on the River Thames between Oxford and Cambridge universities. It has been held since 1829.

stem: Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson is one of the UK's most successful athletes. In which Paralympic sport did she win 11 gold medals?
options: *Wheelchair racing | Wheelchair basketball | Swimming | Archery
explanation: Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson is a famous Paralympic athlete who won 11 gold medals in wheelchair racing. She also won the London Marathon six times.

stem: How many players are there on each team in a Rugby Union match?
explanation: Rugby Union is played by teams of 15 players, while Rugby League is played by teams of 13 players. Both types of rugby are popular in the UK.

stem: In which Olympic sport has the UK won more gold medals than any other country?
options: *Sailing | Swimming | Gymnastics | Football
explanation: The UK has a very successful history in sailing and has won more Olympic gold medals in this sport than any other nation.

stem: Which British athlete won the heptathlon gold medal at the London 2012 Olympic Games?
options: *Jessica Ennis | Kelly Holmes | Paula Radcliffe | Sally Gunnell
explanation: Jessica Ennis (now Jessica Ennis-Hill) won the heptathlon gold medal at the London 2012 Olympic Games. She was one of the famous stars of those Games.

stem: Where is the Millennium Stadium, which hosts Welsh national rugby and football matches, located?
options: *Cardiff | Swansea | Newport | Bangor
explanation: The Millennium Stadium (now also known as the Principality Stadium) is located in Cardiff, Wales. It is the home of Welsh rugby and has also hosted major football matches.

stem: Which golf tournament is the only Major played outside the United States?
options: *The Open Championship | The Masters | The US Open | The PGA Championship
explanation: The Open Championship (often called the British Open) is the oldest golf tournament in the world and the only Major played outside the US.

stem: Which TWO of the following statements about the Commonwealth Games are correct?
options: *They are held every four years. | Only countries from Europe can take part. | They are also known as the Paralympic Games. | *Athletes from Commonwealth countries compete.
explanation: The Commonwealth Games are held every four years. Athletes from Commonwealth nations across the world compete in many different sports.

stem: Which TWO of the following are national football stadiums in the UK?
options: *Wembley in London | *Hampden Park in Glasgow | Silverstone in Northamptonshire | Ascot in Berkshire
explanation: Wembley Stadium in London is the home of English football, and Hampden Park in Glasgow is the home of Scottish football.

stem: Football is the most popular sport in the UK.
options: *True | False
explanation: Football is the UK's most popular sport. It has a massive following across all four nations, with many professional clubs.

stem: Lawn tennis was first played in the UK in the late 19th century.
options: *True | False
explanation: Lawn tennis was first played in the UK in the late 19th century. The famous Wimbledon Championships began shortly after in 1877.

stem: What is the currency of the UK?
options: *The pound sterling | The euro | The dollar | The franc
explanation: The UK currency is the pound sterling. There are 100 pence in a pound.

stem: Which language is spoken by many people in Wales, alongside English?
options: *Welsh | Gaelic | Cornish | Manx
explanation: Many people in Wales speak Welsh, and children learn it at school. In parts of Scotland some people speak Gaelic.

stem: Women make up about half of the workforce in Britain today.
options: *True | False
explanation: Women in Britain have the same rights to work as men. Today they make up about half of the workforce.

stem: What is the traditional national flower of Scotland?
options: *Thistle | Rose | Daffodil | Shamrock
explanation: The thistle is the national flower of Scotland. The rose is for England, the daffodil is for Wales, and the shamrock is for Northern Ireland.

stem: Why is the Welsh dragon not represented on the Union Flag?
options: *Wales was already united with England when the first flag was made | Wales did not want to be represented on the flag | The dragon was considered too difficult to paint | Wales had a different patron saint at that time
explanation: The Welsh dragon does not appear on the Union Flag because Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created in 1606.

stem: How is the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) chiefly funded?
options: *By a TV licence paid by households | By selling advertising space | By direct taxes from the government | By public donations
explanation: The BBC is funded mainly by a TV licence fee paid by households. Because of this, BBC television and radio stations do not show commercial adverts.

stem: What is the minimum age to buy alcohol in a pub or shop in the UK?
explanation: You must be at least 18 years old to buy alcohol in the UK. It is also against the law for anyone under 18 to drink alcohol in a pub.

stem: At what age can a person drink beer, wine, or cider with a meal in a pub if an adult buys it?
explanation: People aged 16 or 17 can drink beer, wine, or cider with a meal in a pub if they are with an adult and the adult buys the drink.

stem: In the UK, what must a dog wear when it is in a public place?
options: *A collar showing the owner's name and address | A bright red jacket | A lead of less than one metre | A special muzzle
explanation: All dogs in public places must wear a collar showing the owner's name and address. Owners can be fined if their dog does not have this.

stem: Which type of British newspaper is generally more serious and contains more detailed news?
options: *A broadsheet | A tabloid | A daily blog | A weekly comic
explanation: Broadsheets (such as The Times) are larger newspapers that publish more serious and detailed news. Tabloids are smaller and focus more on celebrity news.

stem: What is the minimum age at which a person can legally drive a car or motorcycle in the UK?
explanation: You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car or ride a motorcycle on public roads in the UK, provided you have a provisional licence.

stem: Which pop music group from Liverpool became famous worldwide in the 1960s?
options: *The Beatles | The Rolling Stones | The Who | Led Zeppelin
explanation: The Beatles, who came from Liverpool, became one of the most famous and successful music groups in history during the 1960s.

stem: Which ancient language, related to Welsh and Irish, is still spoken by a small number of people in Cornwall?
options: *Cornish | Scots | Gaelic | Manx
explanation: Cornish is a Celtic language spoken by a small number of people in Cornwall, in the south-west of England.

stem: Which TWO of the following are national parks in England?
options: *The Peak District | *Dartmoor | Snowdonia | Loch Lomond and the Trossachs
explanation: The Peak District and Dartmoor are national parks located in England. Snowdonia is in Wales, and Loch Lomond is in Scotland.

stem: Admission to major national museums and art galleries in the UK is usually free.
options: *True | False
explanation: Entry to major national museums and art galleries in the UK is free of charge, although visitors are often asked to make a voluntary donation.

stem: The majority of people in the UK who state a religion in the census identify as Christian.
options: *True | False
explanation: According to census data, Christianity remains the most common religion in the UK, although many people state they have no religion.

stem: Which of these is the traditional national flower of Northern Ireland?
options: The Rose | *The Shamrock | The Daffodil | The Thistle
explanation: The shamrock is the symbol of Northern Ireland. It is a plant with three green leaves that is linked to the patron saint, St Patrick.

stem: Which TWO of these languages are spoken by some people living in Scotland?
options: *Gaelic | *Scots | Welsh | Cornish
explanation: Gaelic is a minority language spoken in parts of Scotland. Scots is a language related to English spoken by many people across the country.

stem: Which BBC radio station focuses on news, drama, and talk shows rather than music?
options: Radio 1 | Radio 2 | Radio 3 | *Radio 4
explanation: BBC Radio 4 is well known for its news and talk programmes. BBC Radio 3 is a station that mainly plays classical music.

stem: In a traditional British pub, people usually wait at their table for a waiter to come and take their drink order.
options: True | *False
explanation: Customers usually go to the bar to order and pay for their drinks. In many pubs, you can also order your food at the bar.

stem: What type of newspaper has small pages and often focuses on celebrity news and gossip?
options: A broadsheet | *A tabloid | A journal | A chronicle
explanation: Tabloids use a smaller page size and have many stories about famous people. Broadsheets are larger and focus more on serious news.

stem: What is the minimum age to enter a betting shop or a casino in the UK?
options: 16 years old | *18 years old | 21 years old | 25 years old
explanation: You must be at least 18 years old to gamble or enter gambling premises. This law helps to protect children and young people.

stem: Which of these flowers is the traditional national symbol of England?
options: *The Rose | The Daffodil | The Thistle | The Shamrock
explanation: The rose is the national flower of England. The daffodil and the leek are the traditional symbols used for Wales.

stem: The UK constitution is written down in a single document.
options: True | *False
explanation: The UK constitution is not written in one document, so it is often called 'unwritten'. It comes from laws, conventions and court decisions.

stem: What type of monarchy does the UK have?
options: *A constitutional monarchy | An absolute monarchy | An elected monarchy | A military monarchy
explanation: In a constitutional monarchy the king or queen does not rule the country. The elected government makes decisions.

stem: Who is the head of state of the UK?
options: *The monarch | The Prime Minister | The Speaker of the House of Commons | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The monarch is the head of state. The Prime Minister is the head of the government.

stem: What does the Speaker of the House of Commons do?
options: *Chairs debates and keeps order, staying neutral | Leads the government | Speaks for the monarch | Leads the opposition
explanation: The Speaker is an MP chosen by other MPs. The Speaker chairs debates, keeps order and does not take sides.

stem: Who sits in the House of Commons?
options: *Members of Parliament elected by voters | Peers appointed for life | Senior judges | Bishops of the Church of England
explanation: The House of Commons is made up of MPs elected by voters in their constituencies. It is the more important of the two Houses.

stem: How often must a general election be held?
options: *At least every five years | Every four years | Every three years | Every seven years
explanation: A general election must be held at least every five years. MPs are elected in every constituency.

stem: When a new law is being discussed in Parliament, what is it called before it is passed?
options: *A Bill | A Decree | A Petition | A Charter
explanation: A Bill is a proposed law. After it is passed by Parliament and given Royal Assent, it becomes an Act of Parliament.

stem: What is the group of senior ministers who help the Prime Minister make important decisions?
options: *The Cabinet | The Assembly | The Council | The Senate
explanation: The Cabinet consists of about 20 senior ministers. They lead government departments and discuss important policies.

stem: Which TWO are the main chambers of the UK Parliament?
options: *House of Commons | *House of Lords | House of Representatives | House of Assembly
explanation: The UK Parliament is made up of the House of Commons, the House of Lords, and the Monarch. Both houses must usually agree on a law.

stem: Judges in the UK are independent of the government and should not be influenced by politicians.
options: *True | False
explanation: Judges are not politicians and cannot be dismissed by the government because of their decisions. This keeps the legal system fair.

stem: Who is the leader of the political party with the second-largest number of seats in the House of Commons?
options: *The Leader of the Opposition | The Deputy Prime Minister | The Lord Speaker | The Home Secretary
explanation: The Leader of the Opposition leads the second-largest party. Their role is to challenge and question the government's work.

stem: What is the main responsibility of the "executive" branch of the UK government?
options: *Carrying out the laws | Making the laws | Interpreting the laws | Running the court system
explanation: The executive is the branch of government that carries out policies. This includes the Prime Minister and their Cabinet.

stem: Who appoints the Prime Minister?
options: *The Monarch | The House of Commons | The voters | The House of Lords
explanation: After a general election, the Monarch asks the leader of the party with the most members in the House of Commons to form a government.

stem: Which TWO of the following sit in the House of Lords?
options: *Hereditary peers | *Life peers | Members of Parliament (MPs) | Local councillors
explanation: Life peers are chosen for their experience and stay for life. Hereditary peers are members who inherited their title from their family.

stem: The Prime Minister is the person who leads the government.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Prime Minister is the head of the government. The Monarch is the head of state but does not have political power.

stem: What are the senior members of the main opposition party called when they mirror the roles of government ministers?
options: *The Shadow Cabinet | The High Court | The Civil Service | The Privy Council
explanation: Members of the Shadow Cabinet look at the work of government ministers. They propose different ideas and policies for their party.

stem: What must happen before a bill can become an Act of Parliament?
options: *It must get Royal Assent | It must be signed by the public | It must be approved by the UN | It must be reviewed by judges
explanation: Royal Assent is when the Monarch formally agrees to a bill. This is now a formality and the Monarch does not refuse to sign.

stem: Who works for the government but remains neutral and does not change when a new party is elected?
options: *Civil servants | Cabinet ministers | Members of Parliament | Local councillors
explanation: Civil servants are permanent staff who help the government. They must be politically neutral and give honest advice to ministers.

stem: What does "Parliamentary Sovereignty" mean?
options: *Parliament has the power to make any law | The Monarch makes the laws | The Prime Minister is above the law | Only judges can change laws
explanation: Parliamentary Sovereignty means Parliament is the highest legal authority. It can pass or change any law it chooses.

stem: Where do the most senior members of the Church of England sit in the UK Parliament?
options: *The House of Lords | The House of Commons | The Supreme Court | The Cabinet
explanation: Some senior bishops and archbishops of the Church of England sit in the House of Lords. They are known as the Lords Spiritual.

stem: Members of the House of Lords are elected by the public in a general election.
options: True | *False
explanation: Members of the House of Lords are appointed or inherited, not elected. Only members of the House of Commons are elected by the public.

stem: Which of these sources forms part of the unwritten UK constitution?
options: *Acts of Parliament | A single written constitution document | Rules set by local councils | Treaties signed by foreign mayors
explanation: The UK constitution comes from several sources, including Acts of Parliament, common law, and unwritten conventions. It is not written in a single document.

stem: What happens during the annual State Opening of Parliament?
options: *The monarch reads a speech written by the government | Members of Parliament elect a new Prime Minister | Judges explain new legal decisions to the public | Citizens vote on proposed laws for the coming year
explanation: At the State Opening of Parliament, the monarch reads the King's or Queen's Speech. This speech outlines the government's plans and proposed laws for the upcoming session.

stem: Where is the Scottish Parliament located?
options: *Edinburgh | Glasgow | Aberdeen | Dundee
explanation: The Scottish Parliament is located in Holyrood, Edinburgh. It was established in 1999 to make laws on devolved matters for Scotland.

stem: Which TWO of the following are devolved matters managed by devolved administrations?
options: *Education | *Health services | National defence | Foreign relations
explanation: Education and health services are devolved matters managed separately in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. Defence and foreign affairs remain the responsibility of the UK government.

stem: What is the Welsh name for the Welsh Parliament?
options: *Senedd | Stormont | Holyrood | Whitehall
explanation: The Welsh Parliament is known as the Senedd. It meets in Cardiff Bay and passes laws for Wales on devolved matters.

stem: In which city does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
options: *Belfast | Londonderry | Armagh | Newry
explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast. It makes decisions on devolved local issues in Northern Ireland.

stem: Foreign policy and national defence are reserved to the UK Parliament in London.
options: *True | False
explanation: Reserved matters like foreign policy, defence, and main taxes affect the whole UK and are decided only by the UK Parliament in London.

stem: Members of the House of Lords are permitted to vote in UK general elections.
options: True | *False
explanation: Members of the House of Lords are not allowed to vote in UK general elections. Members of the armed forces and citizens aged 18 or over can vote if registered.

stem: What must a person be registered on to vote in a UK official election?
options: *The electoral register | The national tax database | The census index | The civil service roll
explanation: To vote in any election in the UK, your name must be on the electoral register. You can register online or by post.

stem: What is it called when an elector appoints someone else to cast their vote?
options: *Voting by proxy | Voting by shadow | Voting by cabinet | Voting by motion
explanation: If you cannot vote in person, you can apply for a proxy vote, which allows a named person to vote for you. You can also apply for a postal vote.

stem: Which of these local services is the responsibility of local government councils?
options: *Collecting household rubbish | Controlling national defence | Issuing British passports | Setting national income tax rates
explanation: Local government councils look after local services such as collecting household waste, maintaining local roads, and managing local parks.

stem: Which TWO of the following are examples of pressure groups that try to influence policy?
options: *Trade unions | *Environmental charities | County courts | Government departments
explanation: Pressure groups are organisations that try to influence government policy and decisions. Examples include trade unions, business groups, and environmental charities.

stem: Which law incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?
options: *The Human Rights Act 1998 | The Equality Act 2010 | The Bill of Rights 1689 | The Magna Carta 1215
explanation: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. It allows people to defend their rights in UK courts.

stem: What is the name of the voting system used in UK general elections to the House of Commons?
options: *First-past-the-post | Proportional representation | Single transferable vote | Alternative vote
explanation: In this system, the candidate with the most votes in their local area (constituency) is elected as the MP. They do not need to get more than 50% of the votes to win.

stem: What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
explanation: You must be 18 or over to vote in elections to the UK Parliament. In some elections in Scotland and Wales, people can vote at 16.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In which year did the voting age for everyone become 18?
explanation: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 for men and women in 1969.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In the 1830s and 1840s, the Chartists campaigned for every man to have the right to vote.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Chartists were a group who campaigned for political reform, including votes for every man and secret ballots.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which document signed in 1215 limited the power of the King and protected the rights of the people?
options: *Magna Carta | The Bill of Rights | The Domesday Book | The Act of Union
explanation: Magna Carta was signed in 1215. It was the first document to limit the King's power and state that the monarch must obey the law.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: The UK is a "constitutional monarchy". What does this mean?
options: The King makes all the laws | *The King has limited power by law | The King is elected by the public | The King is also the Prime Minister
explanation: In a constitutional monarchy, the King or Queen is the Head of State but has limited power. The government and Parliament make the laws.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which law, passed in 1689, confirmed that the King or Queen could not make laws without Parliament's agreement?
options: The Great Charter | The Reform Act | *The Bill of Rights | The Habeas Corpus Act
explanation: The Bill of Rights 1689 confirmed Parliament's power. It meant the King could not raise taxes or make laws without the consent of Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What was a major change made by the Reform Act of 1832?
options: It gave women the vote | *It reduced the number of small voting areas | It made the voting age 18 | It gave all men over 18 the vote
explanation: The 1832 Reform Act increased the number of people who could vote. It also removed 'pocket boroughs', which were areas with very few voters.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: In which year did women in the UK get the same voting rights as men?
explanation: In 1918, some women got the vote, but they had to wait until 1928 for equal voting rights. Since 1928, all men and women over 21 could vote.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Who was the leader of the Suffragette movement in the early 20th century?
options: Florence Nightingale | *Emmeline Pankhurst | Margaret Thatcher | Mary Peters
explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst led the Suffragettes. They were a group of women who campaigned strongly for women's right to vote in the early 1900s.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Who is responsible for keeping order during political debates in the House of Commons?
options: The Prime Minister | *The Speaker | The Monarch | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The Speaker is an MP chosen to be neutral. They stay independent of their party to ensure that all points of view are heard in debates.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is a proposed new law called before it is passed by Parliament?
options: An Act | *A Bill | A Petition | A Decree
explanation: A proposed new law is called a Bill. It must be debated and passed by both the House of Commons and the House of Lords to become an Act.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Usually, what is the maximum amount of time between general elections in the UK?
options: Every 3 years | Every 4 years | *Every 5 years | Every 10 years
explanation: General elections for the House of Commons are usually held every five years. The Prime Minister can sometimes choose to hold one earlier.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What name is given to the group of senior ministers who help the Prime Minister lead the country?
options: The Civil Service | *The Cabinet | The Assembly | The Opposition
explanation: The Cabinet consists of about 20 senior ministers. Each minister is usually the head of a government department, such as the Home Office.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the main job of a Member of Parliament (MP) in the UK?
options: To run the local council | *To represent people in their local area | To manage the local police force | To judge cases in a court
explanation: MPs represent every person in their local area, even those who did not vote for them. They handle problems and represent their area in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO parts of the UK have their own devolved parliaments or assemblies?
options: *Scotland | *Wales | England | London
explanation: Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have devolved governments. These governments make decisions on local things like education and health.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO of these are the names of the two houses that make up the UK Parliament?
options: *The House of Commons | *The House of Lords | The House of Senators | The House of Representatives
explanation: The UK Parliament has two parts: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. The Commons is elected, and the Lords is mostly appointed.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: The Habeas Corpus Act was passed in 1679. What does this law protect?
options: The right of the monarch to create new taxes | *The right of a prisoner to be brought before a court | The right of all men over 21 to vote | The right of the government to close Parliament
explanation: This law ensures that no one can be held in prison unlawfully. Every prisoner has the right to go to court to see if their detention is legal.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the name of the voting system used for UK general elections?
options: Proportional Representation | *First Past the Post | Single Transferable Vote | The List System
explanation: The UK uses the 'First Past the Post' system. The candidate who gets the most votes in their local area (constituency) wins the seat in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What happens if an MP dies or resigns before the next general election?
options: The seat remains empty until the next general election | The Prime Minister chooses a new representative | The local council votes for a replacement | *A by-election is held in that area
explanation: A by-election is held to find a new representative for that specific area. This ensures the people living there still have a voice in Parliament.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which group is formed by the second-largest party in the House of Commons?
options: The Cabinet | The Civil Service | *The Shadow Cabinet | The Privy Council
explanation: The second-largest party is called the official Opposition. Their leader forms a 'Shadow Cabinet' to monitor and challenge government ministers.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Which TWO of these are true about civil servants in the UK?
options: *They are politically neutral | They are elected by the public | *They keep their jobs when the government changes | They are members of the House of Lords
explanation: Civil servants must be neutral and not take sides in politics. They work for the government and keep their jobs even when a new party is elected.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: Most major government departments are led by a senior politician known as a Secretary of State.
options: *True | False
explanation: A Secretary of State is a senior minister in the Cabinet. They are responsible for a specific area of work, such as health, education or defence.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the name of the daily record that lists everything said in Parliament?
options: The Magna Carta | *Hansard | The Bill of Rights | The Daily Gazette
explanation: Hansard is the official report of all debates in the House of Commons and the House of Lords. It can be read online or in libraries.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The development of British democracy

stem: What is the Prime Minister's official home in London?
options: *10 Downing Street | 11 Downing Street | Buckingham Palace | Lambeth Palace
explanation: The Prime Minister lives and works at 10 Downing Street. The Prime Minister also has a country house called Chequers.

stem: Which government minister is responsible for the economy?
options: *The Chancellor of the Exchequer | The Home Secretary | The Foreign Secretary | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy. The Home Secretary deals with crime, policing and immigration.

stem: What is the second-largest party in the House of Commons usually called?
options: *The opposition | The cabinet | The civil service | The coalition
explanation: The second-largest party is the opposition. Its leader is the Leader of the Opposition, who leads a shadow cabinet.

stem: Civil servants must be politically neutral.
options: *True | False
explanation: Civil servants carry out government policy. They do not take sides and keep working for the new government after an election.

stem: What is the official record of what is said in Parliament called?
options: *Hansard | The Domesday Book | The Gazette | The Magna Carta
explanation: Hansard is the official report of what is said in Parliament. Anyone can read it, and debates are also broadcast.

stem: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
options: *Stormont, in Belfast | Holyrood, in Edinburgh | Westminster, in London | Cardiff Bay, in Cardiff
explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont in Belfast. It has powers over matters such as health and education.

stem: Where is the Scottish Parliament?
options: *Holyrood, in Edinburgh | Glasgow city centre | Stormont, in Belfast | Westminster, in London
explanation: The Scottish Parliament meets at Holyrood in Edinburgh. It can make laws for Scotland on many matters.

stem: In the United Kingdom, who is the ceremonial head of state?
options: The Prime Minister | *The Monarch | The Speaker | The Lord Chancellor
explanation: The Monarch is the head of state but does not rule the country. The government is led by the Prime Minister.

stem: General elections for the UK Parliament must be held at least every how many years?
options: 3 years | 4 years | *5 years | 10 years
explanation: General elections for the House of Commons must happen at least every five years. The Prime Minister decides the exact date.

stem: To vote in a UK General Election, a person must be at least 18 years old on the day of the election.
options: *True | False
explanation: You must be 18 to vote in a General Election. In some parts of the UK, 16-year-olds can vote in local or devolved elections.

stem: What is the name of the list that contains the names of everyone who is allowed to vote?
options: The Census | *The Electoral Register | The National Record | The Social Security List
explanation: The Electoral Register is a list of names of everyone who has signed up to vote. It is updated every year.

stem: Which TWO services are usually provided by local councils?
options: *Fire services | National defence | *Public libraries | Foreign policy
explanation: Local councils provide many everyday services. These include education, social services, and the disposal of rubbish.

stem: What is the name given to the group of senior politicians who lead government departments?
options: The Privy Council | The Civil Service | *The Cabinet | The House of Lords
explanation: The Cabinet is a group of about 20 senior ministers. They make the most important decisions about how the country is run.

stem: The UK is one of five permanent members of which international group?
options: The European Union | *The UN Security Council | NATO | The G7
explanation: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council. This group works to keep peace and security in the world.

stem: In the UK, every person who is eligible to vote must register to do so individually.
options: *True | False
explanation: Each person must register themselves to vote. In the past, the head of a household could register everyone living in their home.

stem: Which TWO groups of people are eligible to vote in a UK General Election?
options: *British citizens | Any foreign national living in the UK | Permanent residents from any country | *Irish citizens living in the UK
explanation: To vote in a General Election, you must be a British citizen or a qualifying citizen of Ireland or the Commonwealth.

stem: What is the group of senior opposition MPs who monitor the work of government ministers called?
options: The Backbenchers | *The Shadow Cabinet | The Selection Committee | The Speaker's Office
explanation: The Shadow Cabinet is a group of senior politicians from the main opposition party. They lead the debate against the government.

stem: What is the name of the devolved government building in Wales?
options: *The Senedd | Holyrood | Stormont | Westminster
explanation: The Senedd is the name for the Welsh Parliament. It is located in Cardiff and makes laws for Wales on many local issues.

stem: NATO is an international organisation. What is its main purpose?
options: To promote world trade | *To protect its members by military means | To manage environmental laws | To provide medical aid
explanation: NATO is a group of countries that agree to protect each other if they are attacked. It was formed after the Second World War.

stem: When people from political parties visit houses to ask for votes before an election, it is called canvassing.
options: *True | False
explanation: Canvassing is when party members talk to people on the streets or at their homes. They do this to explain their party's ideas.

stem: Who chairs debates in the House of Commons and keeps order?
options: *The Speaker | The Prime Minister | The Lord Chancellor | The Chief Whip
explanation: The Speaker is an MP chosen by other MPs to chair debates in the House of Commons. The Speaker must remain politically neutral and does not vote.

stem: Which statement about the British constitution is correct?
options: *It is not written down in a single document | It was written in a single document in 1945 | It can only be changed by a national referendum | It cannot be amended by Parliament
explanation: The UK constitution is uncodified, meaning it is not set out in a single document. Instead, it is formed of statutes, court judgments, and traditions.

stem: In a UK General Election, the voting system used is called first-past-the-post.
options: *True | False
explanation: Under the first-past-the-post system, the candidate who receives the most votes in each constituency is elected as the Member of Parliament.

stem: Which government minister is responsible for policing and national security?
options: *The Home Secretary | The Foreign Secretary | The Defence Secretary | The Justice Secretary
explanation: The Home Secretary leads the Home Office and is responsible for crime prevention, policing, and national security in the UK.

stem: Which TWO ways can people cast their vote in a UK general election?
options: *In person at a polling station | *By post | By sending a text message | By voting on an official website
explanation: Voters can cast their ballot in person at a polling station, by post, or by proxy by appointing someone to vote on their behalf.

stem: Which version of the electoral register can be bought by anyone and used for marketing?
options: *The open register | The full register | The civic register | The national register
explanation: The open register can be purchased by businesses and individuals for marketing. Voters can ask to have their names excluded from it.

stem: Which government minister is responsible for UK relations with foreign countries?
options: *The Foreign Secretary | The Home Secretary | The International Trade Secretary | The Defence Secretary
explanation: The Foreign Secretary is responsible for managing the UK's relations with other countries and leading the diplomatic service.

stem: Which TWO types of members sit in the House of Lords?
options: *Life peers | *Hereditary peers | Civil servants | Local councillors
explanation: The House of Lords is made up of life peers, hereditary peers, and senior Church of England bishops. Members are not elected.

stem: The 1998 Good Friday Agreement led to the creation of the Northern Ireland Assembly.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly was created following the Good Friday Agreement in 1998 to provide power-sharing between communities.

stem: Which area of policy has been devolved to the Welsh government?
options: *Education and health | Defence and armed forces | Immigration control | Foreign affairs
explanation: The Welsh government has powers over areas such as education, health, and transport, while defence and foreign policy remain with the UK government.

stem: Who does the monarch appoint as Prime Minister after a General Election?
options: *The leader of the party that wins the most seats | The longest-serving Member of Parliament | The candidate who received the most public votes | A senior politician chosen by the House of Lords
explanation: The monarch invites the leader of the political party that commands a majority in the House of Commons to form a government as Prime Minister.

stem: At which stage of a bill is it examined in detail by a committee of MPs?
options: *The committee stage | The first reading | The second reading | The Royal Assent
explanation: During the committee stage, a bill is examined line by line by a committee of MPs, and changes called amendments can be suggested.

stem: What are the MPs who make sure members of their party attend votes called?
options: *Whips | Ushers | Clerks | Serjeants
explanation: Whips are MPs or peers chosen by their party to organise voting and make sure that party members turn up and vote with their leadership.

stem: The UK is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council, which works to keep international peace and security.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is the Commonwealth?
options: *An association of countries, most once part of the British Empire | A group of European countries that trade freely | A military alliance of North Atlantic countries | The parliament of the four UK countries
explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of countries. Most were once part of the British Empire, and the monarch is its head.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is NATO?
options: *A group of countries that agree to defend each other | A group of countries that share one currency | A charity that helps refugees | A court that settles trade disputes
explanation: The UK is a member of NATO, a group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if they are attacked.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Which organisation created the European Convention on Human Rights?
options: *The Council of Europe | The United Nations | The Commonwealth | NATO
explanation: The Council of Europe created the European Convention on Human Rights. It is separate from the European Union.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Who is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth?
options: *The British Monarch | The Prime Minister | The Secretary of State | The President of the UN
explanation: The Monarch is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth. Most member countries were once ruled by Britain but are now independent.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: How often are the Commonwealth Games held?
options: Every 2 years | *Every 4 years | Every 5 years | Every 10 years
explanation: The Commonwealth Games take place every four years. Athletes from all member countries come together to compete in various sports.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: How many member countries are there in the United Nations Security Council in total?
options: 5 members | 10 members | *15 members | 25 members
explanation: The Security Council has 15 members. There are five permanent members and ten other members who are elected for two-year terms.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Which TWO of these are values that all Commonwealth member countries agree to follow?
options: *Democracy | *Rule of law | Using the same currency | Having the same religion
explanation: The Commonwealth is based on shared values like democracy and the rule of law. It also works to support human rights and development.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: In which city is the European Court of Human Rights located?
options: London | Brussels | *Strasbourg | Geneva
explanation: The European Court of Human Rights is in Strasbourg, France. It was set up to make sure countries follow the Human Rights Convention.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Joining the Commonwealth is a voluntary choice for a country.
options: *True | False
explanation: Membership of the Commonwealth is voluntary. Countries choose to join to work together on common goals and values.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: In the United Nations General Assembly, how many votes does each country have?
options: *One vote | Two votes | Votes based on population | Votes based on wealth
explanation: In the General Assembly, every member country has one vote. This assembly is where all UN members can discuss global issues.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Which TWO of these international groups is the UK a member of?
options: *The G7 | *The G20 | The African Union | The Arab League
explanation: The UK is part of the G7 and G20. These groups involve the world's largest economies discussing money and security matters.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What was the European Union (EU) called when it was first created?
options: *The European Economic Community | The Council of Europe | The European Peace Project | The Trade Union
explanation: The EU began as the European Economic Community (EEC). It was originally formed by six countries to help trade after World War II.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: The Council of Europe has the power to make laws that all member countries must follow.
options: True | *False
explanation: The Council of Europe cannot make laws. Instead, it creates agreements for countries to follow regarding human rights and democracy.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is the main purpose of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)?
options: To lead military missions | *To promote economic growth | To run the Olympic Games | To manage the world's banks
explanation: The OECD aims to improve the economy and social well-being of people around the world. The UK was a founding member in 1961.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: What is the main rule of NATO regarding a member country being attacked?
options: Other members must stay neutral | Members can choose to help or not | *An attack on one is an attack on all | The UN must give permission to help
explanation: NATO is built on the idea of collective defence. This means if one member is attacked, all other members will help defend them.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Which TWO of these are agencies that are part of the United Nations?
options: *UNICEF | *WHO | NATO | The Commonwealth
explanation: UNICEF (for children) and WHO (for health) are both UN agencies. The UN has many departments that work on specific global problems.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Who is the official that leads the work of the Commonwealth?
options: *The Secretary-General | The Foreign Secretary | The Lord Chancellor | The Speaker
explanation: The Commonwealth Secretariat is led by the Secretary-General. They help manage the meetings and work of the whole organisation.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: The UK is a member of the G7. What is the main purpose of this group?
options: *To discuss global issues like the economy | To manage the Commonwealth Games | To create laws for all member states | To select the leader of the United Nations
explanation: The G7 is a group of countries with large, developed economies. The leaders of these countries meet every year to talk about important issues like the environment and security.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Where is the International Court of Justice located?
options: *The Hague, Netherlands | New York, USA | Brussels, Belgium | Paris, France
explanation: The International Court of Justice is one of the main parts of the United Nations. It is based in the city of The Hague.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: The United Nations (UN) was set up after the Second World War to help keep world peace.
options: *True | False
explanation: The UN was created in 1945 to help countries solve problems by talking rather than fighting. It also works to protect human rights across the world.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · The UK and international institutions

stem: Who usually hears cases in a magistrates' court in England and Wales?
options: *Magistrates, who are usually unpaid volunteers | A judge and a jury | Police officers | Members of Parliament
explanation: Most minor criminal cases are heard by magistrates. They are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications.

stem: How many people sit on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
explanation: A jury has 12 people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland a jury has 15 people.

stem: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court hears cases against people aged 10 to 17?
options: *A youth court | The Crown Court | A county court | The small claims court
explanation: Young people aged 10 to 17 accused of a crime are usually tried in a youth court. Scotland uses a Children's Hearings System.

stem: Which TWO of these are criminal offences in the UK?
options: *Carrying a weapon in public | *Selling tobacco to someone under 18 | Not paying back a loan to a friend | Breaking a contract with a builder
explanation: Carrying a weapon and selling tobacco to under-18s are crimes. Unpaid debts and broken contracts are usually settled under civil law.

stem: A disagreement about faulty goods bought from a shop is usually dealt with under civil law.
options: *True | False
explanation: Civil law covers disputes between people or businesses, such as faulty goods, debts and housing. Criminal law covers crimes.

stem: What do Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) do?
options: *Make sure local police are run well | Decide sentences in court | Write new criminal laws | Train police officers
explanation: PCCs are elected by the public in police areas in England and Wales. They set local police priorities and make sure policing is effective.

stem: Forcing someone to marry is a criminal offence in the UK.
options: *True | False
explanation: A forced marriage is one where someone does not agree to it. It is a crime, and courts can also issue orders to protect people at risk.

stem: How many people sit on a jury in a criminal trial in Scotland?
explanation: In Scotland, a criminal trial jury has 15 members. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, a jury has 12 members.

stem: Which verdict can a Scottish jury give that is NOT available in England and Wales?
options: *Not proven | Guilty with reason | Dismissed | Conditional
explanation: Scottish criminal courts can give three verdicts: guilty, not guilty, or not proven. Courts in England and Wales only use guilty or not guilty.

stem: Which court hears serious criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
options: County Court | *Crown Court | High Court | Youth Court
explanation: Serious criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are decided in the Crown Court before a judge and a jury.

stem: Which TWO of these are disputes covered by civil law?
options: *A disagreement between neighbours about property borders | Robbing a local convenience store | *A dispute over an employment contract | Driving a motor vehicle without insurance
explanation: Civil law covers private legal disputes like property boundary conflicts and breach of contract. Driving without insurance and robbery are criminal offences.

stem: In the UK, the police service is independent of government control.
options: *True | False
explanation: UK police officers are independent of political parties and government control. They must enforce the law without bias.

stem: In Northern Ireland, minor criminal cases are heard in which court?
options: High Court | Sheriff Court | *Magistrates' Court | Crown Court
explanation: Minor criminal offences in Northern Ireland are dealt with in Magistrates' Courts, similar to England and Wales.

stem: Which court deals with most civil law cases in England and Wales?
options: Crown Court | *County Court | High Court of Justiciary | Magistrates' Court
explanation: The County Court handles most civil disputes in England and Wales, such as unpaid debts and housing problems.

stem: Which TWO rights do you have if you are arrested and taken to a police station?
options: *Free legal advice from a solicitor | The right to choose your police officer | The right to go home whenever you choose | *Having someone told where you are
explanation: If you are arrested, you have the right to get free legal advice and to have a friend or family member told about your arrest.

stem: What is the maximum limit for a small claim in England and Wales?
explanation: In England and Wales, the small claims procedure handles simple civil claims up to £10,000.

stem: What is a main role of Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs)?
options: To try serious criminal cases in court | *To patrol streets and prevent crime | To write laws for local councils | To conduct international police investigations
explanation: PCSOs work on the streets to support regular police officers, answer local questions, and deter minor crime.

stem: UK judges must follow instructions given directly by government ministers.
options: True | *False
explanation: Judges in the UK are completely independent of the government. Ministers cannot tell judges how to rule on legal cases.

stem: Which court hears the most serious criminal cases in Scotland?
options: *High Court of Justiciary | County Court | Crown Court | Magistrates' Court
explanation: The High Court of Justiciary in Scotland hears the most serious criminal offences, such as murder.

stem: What financial help may be available to pay for legal costs if you have a low income?
options: *Legal Aid | Crown Grant | Court Relief | Council Tax Benefit
explanation: Legal Aid is a government scheme that can help cover legal expenses for people who qualify based on income and need.

stem: Who should you contact if you want to make a complaint about the police in Scotland?
options: *The Police Investigations and Review Commissioner | The Independent Office for Police Conduct | The Police Ombudsman | The Scottish Parliament
explanation: In Scotland, complaints about the police are handled by the Police Investigations and Review Commissioner (PIRC). This helps to ensure that investigations are fair and independent.

stem: What is the main purpose of the organisation called Crimestoppers?
options: *To let people report crimes anonymously | To provide free legal defence in court | To help victims of crime find housing | To train new police officers
explanation: Crimestoppers is an independent charity. You can contact them by phone or online to report details of a crime without giving your name.

stem: In the UK, how old must a car be before it needs an MOT test to show it is safe to drive?
options: *Three years old | One year old | Five years old | Ten years old
explanation: Cars must have an MOT test every year once they are three years old. It is a criminal offence to drive a car without a valid MOT certificate.

stem: Which TWO of these are the main types of lawyers working in the UK?
options: *Solicitors | *Barristers | Magistrates | Coroners
explanation: Solicitors and barristers are the two main types of lawyers in the UK. Solicitors give general advice, while barristers represent people in higher courts.

stem: If you are summoned for jury service in the UK, you must attend unless you have a valid reason to be excused.
options: *True | False
explanation: Jury service is a compulsory civic duty. If you are chosen and fail to attend without a good reason, you can be prosecuted and fined.

stem: What is the UK law regarding Female Genital Mutilation (FGM)?
options: *It is a serious criminal offence | It is allowed with parental consent | It is a civil matter, not a criminal one | It is legal for adults over 18
explanation: FGM is illegal in the UK. It is also against the law to take a girl abroad for FGM, and doing so carries a heavy prison sentence.

stem: Which organisation gives free, confidential, and independent advice on legal and financial matters?
options: *Citizens Advice | The Law Society | The Home Office | The County Court
explanation: Citizens Advice is a charity that helps people resolve their legal, money, and other problems by providing free information and advice.

stem: Which TWO of these are taxes paid by people in the UK?
options: *National Insurance | *Council Tax | Crown Tax | National Border Duty
explanation: National Insurance helps pay for state benefits and pensions. Council Tax is paid to local governments to fund local services like schools and waste collection.

stem: Which telephone number should you use to contact the police for non-emergency situations?
explanation: You should call 101 to report minor crimes or ask the police for advice when it is not an emergency. You should call 999 only in an emergency.

stem: Under UK law, what is the penalty for buying alcohol for someone who is under the age of 18?
options: *You can be prosecuted and fined | You will only receive a verbal warning | There is no penalty if you are a parent | You will lose your driving licence
explanation: It is a criminal offence to buy alcohol for anyone under 18 years old. This is sometimes called proxy purchasing.

stem: In Northern Ireland, complaints about the conduct of police officers are investigated by the Police Ombudsman.
options: *True | False
explanation: The Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland is an independent body that investigates complaints about the police service to ensure fair treatment.

stem: What should you do if you notice suspicious behaviour that might be linked to terrorism?
options: *Report it to the police immediately | Post about it on social media first | Investigate the situation yourself | Do nothing unless a crime happens
explanation: Everyone has a responsibility to help prevent terrorism. You should report any suspicious activity to the police or the anti-terrorist hotline.

stem: Which court in Scotland deals with minor criminal cases?
options: *Justice of the Peace Court | Crown Court | Youth Court | County Court
explanation: Minor criminal cases in Scotland are heard in a Justice of the Peace Court. More serious criminal cases are dealt with in the Sheriff Court or the High Court of Justiciary.

stem: Which court deals with most civil law cases in Scotland?
options: *The Sheriff Court | The County Court | The High Court | The Magistrates' Court
explanation: In Scotland, most civil cases are dealt with in the Sheriff Court. In England and Wales, most civil cases are heard in the County Court.

stem: You only need a TV licence if you watch programmes on a traditional television set.
options: True | *False
explanation: This is false. You need a TV licence to watch or record live TV programmes on any device, including laptops, mobile phones, and tablets.

stem: Which TWO details must a police officer tell you before they search you?
options: *Their name and police station | *The reason for the search | The name of the Chief Constable | Their home address
explanation: Before a police officer searches you, they must tell you their name, police station, and why they are searching you. You also have the right to a record of the search.

stem: People on the electoral register can be asked to serve on a jury.
options: *True | False
explanation: If you are on the electoral register you may be chosen for jury service. You must do it unless you have a good reason.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the electoral register?
options: *The official list of people who can vote | A list of everyone who pays tax | A record of all MPs | A list of council employees
explanation: To vote, your name must be on the electoral register. You can register online or through your local council.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What does National Insurance help pay for?
options: *State benefits and services such as the State Pension | Car insurance | Home insurance against fire | Private health care
explanation: National Insurance contributions help pay for state benefits and services, such as the State Pension and the NHS.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the minimum age to drive a car on UK roads?
explanation: You must be at least 17 to drive a car. You need a driving licence, which you get after passing a driving test.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is one way people can help support their local school in the UK?
options: *By becoming a school governor | By hiring the teachers | By choosing the national curriculum | By setting the local education tax
explanation: Parents and other people in the community can volunteer as school governors. They help to manage the school's budget and plan its future.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the age of criminal responsibility in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
options: *10 years old | 12 years old | 14 years old | 16 years old
explanation: Children aged 10 and over can be prosecuted in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland, the age of criminal responsibility is 12.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the name of the system used to pay tax automatically from your salary?
options: *PAYE (Pay As You Earn) | VAT (Value Added Tax) | Council Tax | National Insurance
explanation: Under the PAYE system, employers take tax directly from their employees' pay. People who are self-employed must pay tax through Self Assessment.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which TWO of these are well-known volunteering or charity groups in the UK?
options: *The National Trust | *Rotary Clubs | The Civil Service | The Cabinet Office
explanation: The National Trust helps protect historic places and nature, while Rotary Clubs perform local community service. Volunteering is a great way to support the community.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: In Scotland, who is responsible for deciding whether to present a criminal case to court?
options: *The Procurator Fiscal | The Crown Prosecution Service | The Chief Constable | The local magistrates
explanation: In Scotland, the Procurator Fiscal decides whether to prosecute someone. In England and Wales, this job is done by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: All households in the UK are encouraged to recycle their waste to protect the environment.
options: *True | False
explanation: Recycling is an important part of looking after the environment. Local councils collect recyclable waste like paper, plastic and glass.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Where can you go to donate blood to help people in hospitals?
options: *To a blood donation session | To a local police station | To a post office | To a town hall
explanation: Giving blood is a vital way to support the community and save lives. Blood donor sessions are run regularly across the UK.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
options: *Individual liberty | Compulsory military service | A state-controlled press | Freedom from paying local taxes
explanation: The fundamental principles of British life include democracy, individual liberty, the rule of law, and mutual respect and tolerance.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: It is illegal to collect money for charity in a public place in the UK without a licence.
options: *True | False
explanation: To collect money for charity in a public place, you must have a street collection permit from the local council or the police.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which animal welfare charity is the oldest in the UK?
options: *RSPCA | PDSA | Blue Cross | Dogs Trust
explanation: The Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) is the oldest animal welfare charity in the UK. It was founded in 1824.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which TWO of these are common roles that volunteers do in the UK?
options: *Working in a charity shop | *Helping the elderly with shopping | Serving on a professional court jury for pay | Writing national laws for Parliament
explanation: Many people volunteer by helping vulnerable neighbours or working in charity shops. Volunteering is a good way to gain new skills.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: If you are self-employed, how do you pay your income tax?
options: *By completing a Self Assessment tax return | Through automatic PAYE from a bank account | By purchasing tax stamps at a post office | By paying a flat cash fee to the local council
explanation: Self-employed people must keep records of their income and expenses, and complete a Self Assessment tax return each year.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is a PTA in the context of UK schools?
options: *Parent-Teacher Association | Public Teaching Academy | Primary Tuition Authority | Professional Training Agreement
explanation: A Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) is a group of parents and teachers who organise activities to raise extra money for a school.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which of these is a well-known youth organisation where volunteers help young people learn skills?
options: *The Scout Association | The National Trust | The Magistrates' Association | The Electoral Commission
explanation: Organizations like the Scout Association and Girlguiding rely on adult volunteers to run activities and teach skills to young people.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the name of the tax paid to your local council to help fund services like rubbish collection and street lighting?
options: *Council Tax | Value Added Tax | National Insurance | Income Tax
explanation: Council Tax is a tax paid by households to local councils. This money is used to pay for local services like rubbish collection, libraries, and street lighting.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the minimum level of car insurance required by law to drive on public roads in the UK?
options: *Third-party insurance | Fully comprehensive insurance | Breakdown insurance | Personal injury insurance
explanation: To drive a car in the UK, you must have at least third-party insurance. This covers any damage or injury you cause to other people or their property.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which government agency must you notify if you buy or sell a car in the UK?
options: *Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) | HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) | The Home Office | The local council office
explanation: All vehicles in the UK must be registered with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). You must notify them if you buy, sell, or modify a vehicle.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is a Neighbourhood Watch scheme in the UK?
options: *A group of local people who work with police to prevent crime | A government service that cleans local streets | A private security company hired by local councils | A school club that teaches children about road safety
explanation: Neighbourhood Watch schemes are run by local volunteers who work with the police. They help reduce crime and make their communities safer.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: What is the role of a school governor or member of a school board in the UK?
options: *To help set the school's direction and manage its budget | To teach lessons when a regular teacher is absent | To inspect all schools in the country for safety | To cook healthy meals for the students
explanation: School governors are volunteers from the local community who help set the school's direction and monitor its budget. They work closely with the headteacher.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: Which TWO of these UK charities focus on protecting nature and historic buildings?
options: *The National Trust | *The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) | The British Red Cross | Shelter
explanation: The National Trust and the RSPB are major conservation charities in the UK. Many people volunteer for them to help protect historic places and wildlife.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community

stem: In the UK, you can be fined up to £1,000 if you do not attend jury service and do not have a good reason.
options: *True | False
explanation: Jury service is a public duty. If you do not attend without a valid excuse, you are committing an offence and can be fined.
handbook_ref: Chapter 5 · Your role in the community
